incident_description:
I am reporting a dangerously defective firework device.  The firework appears to be homemade and was sold unlabeled.  It appears to a mine or fountain and is constructed from a plain, unlabeled, 1 3/4 inch mortar tube, with no base.  Despite being unlabeled, It was sold to my client by a commercial 1.4G fireworks stand [Shelton Fireworks] located in Robertsdale, Alabama.  

Our client attempted to light the device on July 4, 2025 and it exploded instantly striking him in the face and Left eye.  He has had multiple eye and sinus surgeries and has lost sight in his Left eye.  The victim's wife returned to the store and saw that the store had removed these fireworks from the shelves and placed them in a cardboard box labeled "Please DO NOT Touch".  Our law firm has sent a notice of claim and demand to preserve similar firework devices, but I believe that there should be a formal investigation by CPSC and/or ATF.  This firework device was sold at a 1.4G retail location, however, since it was clearly a homemade device, we have not way of knowing at this time if it would qualify as a 1.3G or 1.4G device.  Likewise, since it exploded instantly, all of these devices should be removed from sale ASAP.  Since the store had already taken them off the shelf before we provided notice of our incident, others may have been hurt as well.
justification: The homemade firework's instant explosion caused severe injury, including loss of sight in one eye.

incident_description:
One of the fireworks exploded in the wrong direction and struck my young child, causing a burn injury. Multiple other items we bought were also defective or misfired.

I reported the incident to the store manager and also submitted video and photo evidence to the corporate office. Despite this, I received no response, no refund, and no concern for safety.

The local store manager initially promised to handle it, then disappeared. Im deeply concerned that this faulty product is still being sold and might harm someone else more seriously in the future.

Update 7/23/2025: Clarification of incident:

I submitted two separate videos showing different fireworks purchased from Sky King Fireworks in Sarasota, FL. Both were lit correctly and in the same manner.

In the first video, the firework fired sideways at first, then continued firing upward.

In the second video, the firework fired sideways, tipped over, and one of the projectiles hit my son in the face, causing a burn injury.


The fireworks were part of a store promotion and were placed together on the same display. Unfortunately, I do not remember all of the product names, but I do recall that one of the items was labeled "Migraine".

Sky King Fireworks responded via email but attempted to shift the blame to improper lighting ÃÂ even though both videos clearly show dangerous misfires.

Unfortunately, I do not have a receipt, as I did not think to save it at the time. However, I encourage the CPSC to request store records or footage from Sky King Sarasota. The store manager (Ryen) is aware of the incident and initially promised compensation.

My only goal is to prevent this from happening to another family. The injury could have been far more serious. I hope your investigation leads to proper action and oversight of this product line.
justification: The incident resulted in a burn injury to a child, and the likelihood of similar incidents occurring is high given the company's lack of response and continued sale of faulty products.

incident_description: On March 11, 2025 I purchased a three pack of Coleman brand single use (disposable) 1 pound propane canisters.  On March 13, 2025 I noticed a strong odor of propane gas emanating from within my detached residential garage.  On closer inspection I found one of the aforementioned Coleman propane bottles was the source of the odor, its highly flammable pressurized contents had inexplicably leaked out and the bottle was nearly empty.  I examined the canister and found no recognizable damage or defect.  Prior to purchase the canister had been shelf stored for sale within an indoor climate controlled retail store environment.  After purchase the canister was stored two days within an outdoor non-climate controlled residential detached garage and experienced normal variation in temperature and atmospheric pressure.  While in my possession the canister in question was not subjected to any degree of stress or damage whatsoever.  Upon discovering the defect I returned the item to the retailer from whom it was purchased and was issued a full refund.  I explained to the retailer my concern for public safety in light of the dangerous defect and received a dismissive response.  I have contacted the corporate headquarters of the retailer to more formally express my product safety concerns had have received no response.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the potential for a fire or explosion was high due to the undetected propane leak, warranting a severity level of 2.

incident_description:
I purchased a N.I.B. "universal aluminum fuel tank cell 20 gallon capacity" to utilize on a marine restoration project, after install and filling the tank with fresh gasoline/2 cycle engine oil mixture, while operating the vessel on a public waterway I continually noticed the odor of gasoline and steady decline in the fuel level according to a connected fuel level gauge. Upon inspecting all the hoses and connections with no leakage noted or found, I furthered my search and observed fuel dripping from the side of the tank opposite the outlet fittings in about an eight inch wide area, approx. an inch and a half above the bottom welded seam in the solid metal sheet making up the side panel.
  
I immediately headed for shore and loaded the vessel onto it's trailer removing it from the waterway and quickly as possible drained the remaining fuel into an approved plastic gasoline storage can/container.
I was only able to recover approx. two gallons from at least ten gallons of the fuel stored in the tank.

The leakage is clearly resulting from a defect in material or workmanship of the product and after contacting the distributor where the item was purchased, they show no concern for the situation other than to quickly point out "after 60 days none of our products are eligible for return or exchange".

My fear is that many of these universal fuel tanks have already been manufactured and sold as well as many more will be manufactured and sold without any regard for quality control, adequate inspection or testing to ensure they do not enter the consumer market base knowing they have a potential to leak combustible fuels into the natural environment or into an environment where an ignition source be present resulting in possible loss, injury or death.
No substantial loss or injuries occurred prior to this report being filed on this incident.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant fuel leak, posing a high likelihood of future incidents with potential injuries or environmental damage.

incident_description:
I was operating a trigger-start Bernzomatic TS4000 Torch to light a wood pellet stove.  The torch is mounted to a hand-held gas cylinder.  Normally, in order to light the torch, the red ignition knob must first be turned to the unlock/ON position.  The torch ignites once the unlocked ignition switch is depressed.  Releasing the ignition button automatically extinguishes the flame.  The locking feature of the ignition switch is a safety feature preventing inadvertent ignition.  On this particular evening, I inadvertently depressed the locked/OFF ignition button and the torch ignited.  Releasing the ignition switch did not extinguish the flame because the ignition switch was still in a locked position.   I was holding a flaming torch that I could not shut off.  The torch ignition switch was stuck in the locked position the entire time and even to this day cannot be unlocked.   Finally, to extinguish the flame, I chose the option of unscrewing the torch from the gas cylinder.
Fortunately, there were no injuries.  This event should never have happened.   There should be no way to override a safety feature and ignite a gas torch by pressing the ignition switch which is clearly in the locked position.   To compound the problem there was no way to unlock the ignition switch.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved an unexpected ignition and inability to extinguish the flame, posing a potential hazard.

incident_description:
The consumer indicates that she went to the passenger seat of her vehicle to light a cigarette with a torch lighter that was inside of her purse. The consumer placed the lighter back in her purse and walked to her house for one minute when her neighbour ran to her house informing her that her vehicle was smoking. The consumer ran outside and initially thought the smoke was coming from her opened trunk because it was full of cleaning supplies and cables so she began removing these. While trying to find the source in her trunk she looked up and saw smoke and flames coming from the passenger seat; she ran over and saw the door melted as well as other parts of her vehicle. The consumer immediately realized that the source of the fire was the torch lighter she had placed in her purse a mere two minutes prior so she quickly removed the purse with some towels and tossed it in a ditch.
 
The consumer was able to put the fire out the door. Most of the torch lighter had melted as well as a wallet in her purse, and there was also extensive smoke damage to her vehicle and fire damage.
 
The consumer states that the unit was used approximately twenty times. 
 
The consumer plans on keeping the torch lighter for at least the next thirty days incase an investigation ensues.

I would definitely like to be reimbursed for the value of my car.  I will never be able to sell my car due to the excessive smoke damage as well as the  damage throughout.
justification: Injury occurred due to melted parts of the vehicle, and the likelihood is high as the cause was a torch lighter left in a purse.

incident_description:
On 10/21/2021 I made an on-line purchase of a ÃÂBlue RhinoÃÂ Brass Propane Fuel Level gauge (Item #: 2561089 |Model #: 03003LWS) from Lowes Home Improvement.  The gauge is designed to be installed in-line between a homeownerÃÂs propane gas BBQ and the propane tank for the BBQ.  The gauge is designed to show the amount of propane gas / fuel remaining in the propane tank. I installed the gauge following the package instructions. I don't think they even read my two emails. I sent another email to 'wecare@bluerhino.com' and they responded with: 
I apologize for the confusion. While Blue Rhino does partner on this product it is manufactured and distributed by a different company, 
'Mr. BarBQ'. Their contact information is on the packaging and I have included it below. You can call 1-888-398-8643 or email at orders@mrbarbq.com.   
Blue Rhino apparently wasn't concerned that a product sold under their name may be hazardous, they just passed me on to 'Mr. BarBQ'.
I feel someone really needs to look at the quality control behind the manufacture of this product before someone gets burned or killed from a propane explosion.

incident_description: I purchased a "Gas One" (the company name) model number GS 3400P "dual fuel portable camping stove" online via Home Depot. The stove functioned properly upon initial use but soon exhibited symptomatic propane odors when connected to either aa propane canister of the common one pound type or a 15 pound  "[REDACTED]" propane tank. Upon investigation of the source of the propane leak using  the "soap bubble" technique (involving the application of common dish soap to all connections) I determined that the attached hose connection had developed a significant leak at the pressure regulator, which is constructed of red plastic mounted on what appears to be a brass fitting that itself is attached to the rubber hose connecting  the stove to the propane tank. During the test the pressure regulator valve "blew out" completely, causing an arching flame to shoot out of the regulator and "connect" to the source of ignition which in this case was the stove itself which I had ignited in order to test the system under realistic conditions. The blown pressure regulator caused my clothing, hair, and other objects nearby to temporarily ignite but I managed to extinguish the flames quickly before they caused major damage. I suffered slight burns that did not require medical attention outside of self administered topical treatment that I applied myself. The propane hose and regulator had not been exposed to any adverse conditions, were not in any way damaged, and suffered this "blow out" after moderate and infrequent use. Upon determining that the propane hose was defective I ordered a replacement hose directly from "Gas One" via their website. The hose is listed as "Replacement Propane Converter" (part number 50411) and connected said replacement hose to the stove, operating  under the assumption that the original hose (which had been included with the stove) had somehow been damaged or was a one time defect. A short time later, again after moderate, infrequent use, the same thing happened; the red plastic pressure regulator "blew out", causing a severe propane leak and a sudden burst of flames from the regulator. Again, the source of the ignition was the stove itself. The regulator simply leaks and or blows out completely and spews enough propane to ignite from any source. At any given time this device fails and  exposes the consumer to potential explosions, fire hazards, and severe propane leaks. Prior to discovering this defective device I had noticed that my propane tanks were running empty in a short period of time, indicating that the regulator had been leaking from the beginning of use without my knowledge. The stove itself appears to be functioning properly, it is the hose which is defective, specifically the red plastic pressure regulator. Furthermore, upon investigating the company itself, I discovered that there were other consumers who had experienced the same thing as I had and had complained to the company about their experiences to no avail.
justification: The incident resulted in slight burns to the user, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the repeated incidents with the same product.

incident_description: GarageBoss Gas cans both 5 gallon and the smaller unit as well.  Since my old gas can that does not use the new vapor standards reached end of life after over a decade in use, it seems the new design's from Briggs & Stratton are just not up to snuff.  First - I had one can that split on the side (split outwards - clearly a stress fracture) .  It took a bit of effort to get ahold of them and they sent me a newer design at least.  I still had one of their 'rounder' rather than squared-up units that didn't split.    Last night our power went out due to the storm.  I started to pour the gas and it shot out of the can much like if I had been at a gas station using a pump and got all over the top and part of the side of my generator.  I cleaned that up and was thinking (at 4am with little sleep) that perhaps I needed to push the button and release some of the pressure first.  So leaving item on the ground I pushed the button and it shot gas out everywhere.  This shouldn't be that complicated of an item that it requires a bunch of special steps during a situation like this, but the hazard here is that it's clearly not managing the pressure properly and spraying gas even when the button is depressed.  The current design unlike a traditional design lacks a pressure release.  Since designs have changed I've had these types of units leak gas, and spray gas etc.. a *LOT* more than the old design.  Their biggest plus is near-instant shutoff - when the button works.  Which leads me to complaint #2 - the biggger unit puts out gas too fast to fill my mower like the old style 5Gal did, so I bought a smaller container to use for that and just transfer the gas from the 5 to that.  But the handle button sticks and gas keeps flowing and gets everywhere when I left the product up to stop (because the pressure keeps it going) getting gas all over my mower.  Eventually I started just pressing the button a small amount but now the handle is leaking gas everywhere.    So essentially in this block of text I've described several issues that not only relate to quality, but that are presenting me a hazzard as Gas is being leaked, sprayed, and generally not managed properly by this line of products.  Given how much difficulty there was in reaching them to discuss this, I figured this route may work out better.   I'm not a materials engineer - but it seems to me that if that Gas was expelling like I saw last night and there was even a hot-pavement (which fortunately at 4am there was not) when this flaw happens, the vapors may become ignited.   Your engineers and science trained people can figure out the real dangers - I'm just expressing my concerns, and frustrations because these products lack of quality is causing safety hazzards for me!  My objective here is to hope that you will put sufficient weight behind my concerns and with the appropriate people at their company to get these products quality  and safety issues fixed.  To restarte those issues I've observed - (1) the handle breaking down after use once a week for 3 months to mow, (2) manufacturing quality the one product that had an issue an split (which I will remind they did replace - but how many others are out there - don't need gas from a 5 GAL spilling in the garage) ,  and (3) last but not least and what's prompted me to write all of this now -  pressure spraying of gasoline when the product is being used.  I might add a #4 - when the unit is near fully filled ( I never fill it fully to allow at least a 1/2 gallon of space for vapors) the handle will not twist-lock to the base unit  fully - after pouring some gas into my generator last night and stopping, then trying to resume gas was no leaking from the twist lock area even though I hadn't been handling that - I had to tighten that further.    *NONE* of these issues had I experienced with their prior products that were before all of the new vapor managing re-designs - the new designs on the market are seemingly causing me greater leaks of gas which negates the whole point!    I've invested over $100 in these products trying to get set of Gas cans I can keep around for mowing needs, and especially for the generator when the power all too frequently goes out - but I cannot have gas spraying out all over my equipment, or just (as exemplified above) all over the ground just because I pressed the button to release pressure.  The old designs - I just pop the yellow cover on the back side and pressure was released - no problems.  Besides the spillage, I don't need to have a condition setup where pressure + vapor on a hot day causes gas to expel unexpectedly fast and creates conditions where vapor ignition becomes an issue!
justification: Gas cans failed to manage pressure properly, leading to gas spills and potential fire hazards.

incident_description:
Scepter smart control gasoline can

I was trying to fill my push mower with gasoline. The push button to open the valve is always stiff and hard to push, but this time when it finally opened, gasoline shot out of it straight up into my face and eyes. 

After running inside to flush water in my eyes to stop the burning, I went back out to see what had happened and noticed the can looked a little bloated. Like there was still pressure. 

Since the weather warned up here, I guess pressure built up in the can since its sealed tight. So when I opened the valve with it tipped up to pour into the tank, all of that pressure was suddenly  released. I'm still not entirely sure how it shot straight up unti my face. 

I decided to take a small nail and puncture a hole in the top/back of the can like old gas cans used to have and the moment I did, you could hear the air whooshing out from the pressure still built up. 

The same thing happened to my mom, though thankfully the pressure hadnt built up enough yet to shoot it in her face.
justification: Gasoline shot into face and eyes, causing immediate burning sensation and potential injury.

incident_description:
WARNING TO PARENTS OF YOUNG CHILDREN!! 
My grandson was shopping with his parents fully supervised at the Tsunami Surf Shop at 13523 NC HWY 50, Surf City, NC. 
He is 5 years old and was playing with the toys displayed below the counter at his eye level, where he came in contact with a cigarette lighter in the shape of a toy gun; he held each end of the lighter with both hands and pulled the trigger. Unfortunately he was badly burned. When the person working in the store was notified of the incident, he was very rude, and dismissed the matter as if it were a trivial issue. 
Children should not have ready access to cigarette lighters, especially those that look like toys not to mention displayed near the toys.

Respectfully submitted, 
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in a child being badly burned, warranting a severity level of 3, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the accessible and misleading design of the cigarette lighter.

The new so-called "Greenlight" Diamond brand strike-on-box and strike-anywhere matches are an extremely unsafe product. I don't know if they are using less wood or if the wood is a poor quality, but the matches are extremely breakable. 
We have often found matches in the box that are barely in one piece. Some of them were far too thin to strike without snapping; fortunately we examined them and threw them away, but someone could easily have been injured if they weren't paying attention.
Many times, upon striking a match, the flaming heads have snapped off and flown across the room. One started to burn the wood of my dresser until I threw water on it. Another landed in a pile of clothes and could easily have started a fire. Another actually landed on my head, singed my scalp, and started to burn my hair. incident_description: The lighter exploded spontaneously, as it was sitting on the table. Before the incident, my partner used the lighter to smoke. Then a few minutes after I heard him setting the lighter on the table, I was woken up by a loud pop, and flames covering the table, and a burning smell. The flames extinguished themselves very quickly, so I realized it was the butane from the lighter. The body of the lighter was laying on the floor melted to the carpet with the metal parts missing. The metal parts were recovered in different parts of the room. I was napping right next to the living room table where this happened, and could have been hit by the projected burning plastic. If the table had been cluttered, or if the lighter had exploded near anything flammable (thankfully my table top is glass), we would have had a house fire. If either of us had been holding it, we would have been severely burned. After the shock faded, we did a little research, and found that this type of lighter which is made in China (the clear plastic kind, made by Ignitus), has a recorded history of a design flaw which allows the flame to continue under the metal plate after the button is released, causing the plastic to melt, and igniting the butane. I suspect this is what happened, as the lighter was sitting on a table indoors at room temperature. If I had known about this, I would not have bought it.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant risk of fire and severe burns, hence severity level 2.

incident_description: I bought a two pack of Scripto Aim and Flame lighters at Walmart on 10-2-18. When I got home, I took one (black) out of the pack and tried to light it. I could not get it to light and I continued to try  for a minute or so. Finally, I set in on a table and got out the second lighter (blue) and lit it within 3-4 feet of the black lighter.  When I lit the blue one, a flame shot across the table to the black, non working lighter and it caught on fire. I was able to get it to the sink and get the fire out, but for several minutes afterward, I saw smoke coming out of it. I finally took it outside where I left it for several hours until I was sure the fire was out.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire, making it an 'Incident, No Injury' case. The likelihood is 'possible' as the user's actions (lighting a second lighter nearby) led to the fire.

incident_description: I have a 10 year old son who was under the care of his grandparents while I was I work. I received a call at work that I needed to meet them at the hospital which was in the town where I worked and 40 minutes from where the accident happened. I was told my son blew his hand off with an m-80. I never questioned things just went to care for my child. My son had been at the junk yard with his grandpa that day helping him. I found out my son had seen a couple fireworks probably 6 months prior to the accident. My dads buddy had brought these fireworks over towards the end of 2017. They had been moved but for some reason that day he had found a lighter from a junk car and remembered seeing the fireworks before so he snuck them off with him. When he went home to his grandparents house he waited for his grandma and little brother to go in the house. he then decided to light 1 of 2 fireworks off. My mom heard a very extreme bang and ran for the door and my son met her on the steps with his hand blown apart. She grabbed a towel wrapped his hand, loaded her dog and his brother up and headed for the ambulance shack as she called 911. My dad was given the fireworks and they were called m-80 by the guy who gave them to him. We never questioned anything just focused on my son. He was taken by ambulance to [REDACTED] where he was then life flighted to [REDACTED] by [REDACTED]. My son went into surgery that night and when he came out he no longer had his right thumb,index finger, or middle finger. his hand was pieced back together and they saved what they could. his ring finger was broken and severely damaged and required pins to hold it and much care to save it. His pinky finger is ok. It also burnt many spots on his body and up the side of his face and behind his ear pretty good. We never asked many questions just asked him if he was holding the firework when he lit it and he said no that he lit it on the ground. We then said you must of tried to throw it because thats what made sense. We never got into many of details just excepted the fact that everyone's lifes had changed. We just worried about the care for my son. Last Monday I received a letter from the government about my sons accident and I was instantly scared because it said it was under investigation. with that being said. I then had to ask many of questions about the firework and the details as to what exactly my son did. I asked my mom about the firework she was led to believe was an m-80 well I found out after my sons accident they gave her his shorts and in the other pocket was the 2nd firecracker. She was able provide me with a picture of it and the information off of it. It was at that moment I learned my son lit a recalled firework not an m-80. I then contacted the CPSC to talk about the accident. He had questions he wanted me to ask my son so months after the accident I now know what happened and it makes so much more sense.  The firecracker that was given to my dad was a detonator fp5 not a m-80.   I went over the the day with my son. He said he took the fireworks because he wanted to light them. we have lit fireworks in the past and he knows the proper way and safety behind them. That day he waited for his grandma to go into the house. I have provided pictures of the firework, the coke can is where it was lit and the damage it caused to the car, my sons hand and the worst burn up his face to CPSC and will attach them him if I get the option to.  that day he bent down stood the firecracker on the ground and lit it with his right hand and decided to move it. the fuse burnt 2-4 second. he still had the lighter in his hand. so going over and over how it took place. he lit it touched it and didn't even make it anywhere before it exploded. he dropped the lighter and ran for the door. My son was in shock for sure but they call him a miracle child. he was awake and aware pretty much the whole time he was cared for except surgery. he is blessed to be alive and that he will be ok but his life is forever changed. he is right handed and now has to learn to use both hands. My son has at least has  2 more surgeries ahead of him.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injuries to the child, including loss of fingers and significant burns, but did not result in death.

incident_description:
Propane Torch hose failed. I posted to Harbor Freight on their site:
"FATAL INCIDENT POTENTIAL - The Propane Torch, Item #91033, S.N. 361441753 suffered a hose separation from the tank connection fitting. This separation allowed propane to escape with the potential of severely burning me. Luckily, as soon as the fitting failed, I tossed the hose and hot wand away from the tank to prevent ignition. I have photos and will gladly share them with you or the Consumer Protection Agency. Please correct this manufacturing error before someone is killed or severely injured. Thanks for your time. [REDACTED]"

I followed up with and email :
"One of your SKU 91033 Propane Torches had a malfunction that could possibly cause severe injury or death. The hose separated from the tank connector because the hose was not crimped properly to that connector. I took every precaution to ensure that the hose was never subjected to strain nor had the hose been damaged in any way.
When the hose separated from the connector, I was sprayed with liquid propane gas. I immediately tossed the hose and wand away from me and turned off the gas. This could have been fatal had I turned around with the hose and hot wand in my hand.
The particulars are in the email below. I have attached photos of the unit."

There was no leakage from the fitting before the failure. I had no warning that the fitting would separate. That separation was instantaneous.

Harbor Freight has been less than willing to respond that they are investigating and correcting a manufacturing issue. This failure is documented on Harbor Freight's reviews of the product at least twice. [REDACTED]

Harbor Freight has been unresponsive in ensuring that they are correcting this manufacturing error. I'm trying to prevent a serious injury or death.
justification: The incident resulted in no injury this time, but the potential for severe burns or death was high due to the sudden hose separation and propane leakage.

incident_description:
I am an attorney representing various injured users of the products in USA and Canada.  The fuel cylinders have design defects at the neck (topmost area).  They fail and explode, causing severe burn injuries and horrific deaths.  In discovery the defendant disclosed that the cylinders filled with "MAPP" fuel have a brazing (welding) compound consisting of:  

        Copper (43-47%); Ethylene glycol (5-10%); Nickel (24-27%); Phosphorus (3-4%)

The other cylinders have brazing compound of 100% copper.  The cylinders with the mixed compound are failing on the compound itself for the most part.  All the cylinders are failing on the parent metal as well, but the cylinders with MAPP fail much more often on the brazing compound.  The fix is to recall and remove all the MAPP cylinders entirely.  The "MAPP" cylinders, and only the MAPP, were discontinued in 2008, but there are millions of them still in possession of users worldwide.  Those simply need to be recalled and returned to the manufacturer for safe destruction.  The propane and propylene need to be recalled and manufactured from a thicker metal.  They are presently .021", which is too thin and allows for failures of the parent metal.  The torch attachments need to be recalled to improve the safety features and remove the trigger lock mechanism.
justification: The incident description reports severe burn injuries and deaths due to exploding fuel cylinders, indicating a high severity level and likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description:
06/2016)The consumer has a safety concern about the plastic caps used on the Midwest gas cans. He stated that the caps crack when the can is stored over the winter season. 

The consumer stated that he discovered the issue when he went to mow the lawn for some of his customers in the spring of this year and last year.

The consumer contacted the firm and was sent replacements. He also asked for gaskets to keep the gas from leaking from the cans. The firm sent the caps but did not sent the gaskets. 

7-07-17

Consumer Product Safety Commission
4330 East West Highway
Bethesda, MD  20814-4408

Dear CPSC:

This report details a comedy of misadventures that occurred in May and June 2017, regarding Midwest Can Company Container Specialties, Inc. 10800 West Belmont Avenue, Franklin Park, IL  60131.

From early May 2017 to this moment, a family's  gas can remains unsafely stored, to the knowledge of Midwest Can.  Either the company doesn't care, or sending two rubber gaskets is too complicated for them.

Three of my customers own Midwest gasoline cans.  In spring 2016, two of the black caps that attach the spout to the cans were discovered cracked, assumingly on account of the bitter winter freeze.  I tend to screw the caps on tightly to assure safety for my customers, but don't  have especially strong wrists.

I phoned Midwest Can customer service, received two caps free of charge, with gaskets, and installed them.  Neither of them cracked this past winter, as the representative assured me they wouldn't. This implies that Midwest was aware of the cracking problem.

However, in spring 2017, the third customer's  Midwest Can cap had cracked.  I noticed there was no gasket on her cap, so I made sure to specify to the customer service representative that a gasket was needed in addition to the cap.  When the package arrived, it contained two black caps-   no gaskets!

I phoned customer service to order two gaskets.  Several days later, a postage due notice (not the package) appeared in my mailbox.  A new Midwest employee had erred, so I was told to write "Return to Sender" on the notice. Three days later, a postage due notice appeared with a package, which I could tell were caps.  Again, a representative, [REDACTED] I believe, asked me to return the package unopened to Midwest.

She kept thinking I referred to the "spout," saying, ''The spout doesn't need a gasket." tried earnestly again to explain that I was referring to the rubber ring that fits inside the black gas can cap, the cap that attaches the nozzle to the can, which I'd expect an employee of a gas can company to comprehend.

She then told me that the black cap doesn't  need a gasket.  Although I knew better, I realized that I'd have to wait until the customer was scheduled again to check for leakage. Yet more time passed with an unsafely stored gas can.  Once there, I put the new cap on tightly and turned the can upside down.  Naturally, it leaked without a gasket.
 
Two messages that I left for a manager, Mr. [REDACTED], went unanswered.  While the company seems to have solved the gas can cap problem, I must assume that an untold number of cans remain stored unsafely across the cold reaches of our country.  If a can with a cracked cap tips, or is knocked over by a child or an animal, gasoline will rapidly leak onto the floor.  Just one spark could erupt the premises into flames, in this current case the garage of a $400,000 house.

This matter has now wasted several hours of my time, which I feel I'm due compensation for being that my request for two gaskets was very simple, and could have been sent for 49 cents postage.  Filing a report with the CPSC ought not to be necessary to receive two gaskets, which I'm still waiting for. The filing of this report will be well worth the effort if one home or shed is kept from burning.

The customer service representatives at Midwest Can are in serious need of better training by which they learn the components of their products, and understand how an improperly-stored  gas can may lead to a tremendous safety hazard.  In the case of Mr. [REDACTED], a simple return call could have spared inconveniences  for several other people, especially after I warned him that I planned to report this to the CPSC.

Thank you Consumer Product Safety Commission for your serious analysis of this
Midwest Can gasoline cap situation.

Sincerely,
[REDACTED]
justification: Potential for property damage due to gasoline leaks from cracked caps, though no injuries reported.

incident_description:
My daughter, who is 27, went outdoors with her boyfriend and decided she wanted to smoke a cigarette. She went back into the house to get a lighter and grabbed a GStar Torchzilla wind proof jet flame butane lighter that was sitting on the bar inside the house. As she was returning, she paused in the room leading to the back patio to see if the lighter worked. She clicked the lighter button/switch and noticed it barely had a flame. She let go of the button, tilted the lighter to turn the bottom plastic adjustment lever toward the + for more flame, thinking the flame was off. That is when the plastic piece on the bottom of the lighter that she was turning flew off and a ball of fire ignited in front of her. She gasped and fell to the floor. The fire burned her hair (at the forehead hairline and some at the ends), her face, nose, lips, upper arm and tip of tongue. We immediately took her to the local emergency room and from there they decided she would be transferred via ambulance to a burn hospital in a city 150 miles away because they were not equipped with the staff or facilities to handle burn victims or the possible outcome of the burns. Thankfully the burn facility determined that she suffered mostly first degree and some second degree burns, but said that she was very lucky because it could have been worse. 

We have not been able to find contact information for the manufacturer. After doing a little research, we have found online reviews about the same type of lighter, made by same manufacturer, that describe the lighter leaking butane, and malfunctioning and staying lit even after letting go of the igniter switch. In some reviews people said it caused a fire or burned their clothing or furniture because it remained lit and they didn't realize it. The lighter is described as a "fire hazard" or "dangerous" in several online reviews. Because of the reviews, GStar has also posted disclaimers about the possible hazards of the lighter in an attempt to make it clear that they are not liable for any injuries. To me, this further proves this lighter is unsafe. 

The lighter that caused my daughters injuries was purchased by my husband at a gas station along an interstate highway and they are sold online, as well as at many other convenience stores. When he purchased the lighter it did not come with any literature or warning stickers attached to it. We were unaware of any of the possible dangers associated with this specific lighter. It was not until after the incident that we began to research this information. If the manufacturer knows that there are defects with this lighter, they should not continue to market and sell it.

incident_description: The following incident occurred on the front steps of my home ([REDACTED]) on Friday, April 28, 2017 at approximately 10:15 a.m. I sat down and, after a brief conversation with a yard-worker, went to lite a [REDACTED] cigarette with a blue MK lighter (barcode: 6 945794 710077) recently purchased from a nearby gas station, Little 5 Points Chevron (372 Moreland Ave. Atlanta, GA 30307). I put the cigarette in my mouth and brought the lighter to the right side of my face with my right hand, shielding it--instinctually--with my left. When I rolled my thumb over the grove of the lighter, however, it did not produce a single, low level flame but, instead, exploded into a ball of flame spanning approximately two feet wide by three feet tall. Though I immediately threw the lighter, still aflame, the explosion burned off all of the hair on my right temple, cheek, chin and upper-neck as well as from my inner right arm. It also significantly singled my right eyebrow and eyelashes, my entire hairline as well as the ends of my hair, clipped atop my head. The explosion also noticeably singed, to a lesser degree, to the my left side of my face, eyebrow and eyelashes. The right side of my scalp, temple, cheek, ear, and arm also showed signs of minor burn that felt raw and remained warm to the touch throughout the remainder of the day. Within a minute or two, a neighbor approached and noted my paralyzing shock. After I'd told him what had happened, he retrieved the same blue, MK lighter from the bottom of the cement steps and handed it to me, noting a crack at its base from my throwing it (in attempts to expel the explosion away from my face). In the hour that followed, I contacted Arrow Lighter (the lighter manufacturer associated with HK lighters) and they seemed generally uninterested, failing to even take down my name, the product number or even develop a report. I was especially horrified by this reaction when, through a very basic internet search, I learned of the many, many reports of HK lighter explosions in addition to one death ([REDACTED], a machinist from Stephenville, Texas was only 56 years... His last words, en route to a Dallas hospital, were: ÃÂMy lighter exploded.ÃÂ) I also photo-documented my injuries and met with a Registered Nurse who notated her observations via video. The following day, I returned to the same nearby gas station (Little 5 Points Chevron) and purchased an identical lighter as the one I'd bought a few days before then spoke to the manager about the incident, who relayed that he'd purchased a large batch of MK lighters from Gandhi Wholesale (located, according to further research, at 103 Forest Parkway, Forest Park, GA 30297).
justification: The incident resulted in significant burns and injuries, but no fatalities, and the likelihood of such an event occurring with the same brand of lighter is high given the reported incidents and the manufacturer's lack of interest.

I know I should have got rid of and reported the lighter then.

(since writing this report, I went to get the lighter and can to fill out product information.  The fluid can tip is melted which is why it wouldn't shut off, I believe.)
justification: The incident resulted in significant burns and potential loss of eyebrows and eyelashes, warranting a severity level of 3. The likelihood is high as the incident was caused by a known design flaw in the lighter.

incident_description: I went to fill up my chain saw with gas.  I put the nozzle into the tank, and used the edge of the tank to activate the valve on the end of the nozzle.  As soon as I pressed down, fuel sprayed back at me at a high velocity.  It sprayed on my left arm, chest, and face.  Apparently, since it was a warm day, the gas can became pressurized.  Afterwards, I did read the instructions on the can and it said to vent first.  Not sure that many people would do that.  With the old style cans, they had an easy flip vent, or they vent when you removed the cap.  I thought that the new "safety" styles were just a complete pain to use, since it takes about 5 minutes to empty a 5 gallon can.  I usually take the nozzle off and use a funnel.  I didn't realize these things could also be so dangerous, spraying a lot of atomized fuel back at the user.
justification: High pressure in the gas can due to warm temperature caused fuel to spray back at high velocity, leading to injury.

incident_description:
Instead of the classic spout and vent, the Scepter Eco gas can employs a single opening, with the vent incorporated into the spout.   This vent is opened by rotating a collar.

However, the collar:

incident_description: While minor  was using a TNT Jumbo California Candle, manufactured in China for American Promotional Events, Inc., the back end of the candle exploded causing severe burns to minor's  forearm.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns, classifying it as an injury event, and the likelihood is considered possible given the unexpected explosion of a candle.

incident_description: On 6-23-16 I purchased a pack of 7 pack of Scripto lighters while shopping at Walmart in Princeton, Minnesota. On 6-30-16 at about 10 pm I used one of the lighters out of this package to burn a wood tick I found crawling on me and then set the lighter down on a microwavable plate on top of our countertops. A few minutes later my wife and I heard a loud pop sound. I got up out of bed and while leaving my bedroom I heard a loud "whoosh" sound. I ran to the kitchen area and found that the lighter I had used a few minutes earlier had burst into flames! It burned through the plate it was on and started the countertop on fire! I was able to extinguish the fire with a bath towel. On 7-14-16 I sent certified mail copies of receipt, photos of damage and estimates for new countertops to both Walmart and the CEO of Calico brands  [REDACTED]in Ontario, CA. On 8-25-16 Walmart had their claims department sent me a letter explaining that Calico brands would be responsible for the claim and to contact [REDACTED] at [REDACTED]. I then mailed all of the information to [REDACTED]. I received two phone calls after this from Calico brands employees. I believe I spoke to [REDACTED] and [REDACTED]. In one of the phone calls it was requested that I mail the burnt up lighter, packaging and remaining lighters to Calico brands to have them looked at for flaws. I was never contacted back regarding the defective lighter. I am very concerned for the safety of others regarding these lighters. It should be noted that Calico brands has not sent the defective lighter back to me which was agreed on. I would like this lighter to be looked at by an outside agency.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and the likelihood of occurrence is high given the product's defect and common usage.

incident_description: I was using the Arnold Siphon Pump to transfer gasoline.  After using the product, it started to leak after the glue used to hold together the pump assembly dissolved.  Gasoline spurted from the hand pump creating a very hazardous situation.  This product is advertised to transfer gas, oil, and other liquids.  It is unsuitable and dangerous to transfer gasoline.  I purchased the product at Lowes and after reading reviews on the product after the fact, other consumers have reported the same issue.
justification: The product failed to safely transfer gasoline, leading to a hazardous leak, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: My husband was using one of the see through colored lighters and was tapping it lightly on the table. He was holding the metal end with his fingers and while tapping exploded in his hand. It did not injured him we believe it was based on the angle and where he was holding it but a portion of the side blew out of the lighter. It was unbelievable and took us both a moment to realize what had just happened. We never found the piece that blew out. This is a serious safety hazard.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the explosion of the lighter poses a high risk of injury in future similar incidents.

incident_description:
I am setting in the living room watching t.v. and I hear a sizzling noise coming from my coffee table, it was a green lighter. I picked it up held it to my ear the noise was coming from the lighter, leaking fuel. I broke it up and disposed of it, but what if it exploded and something caught fire my apartment would have burned, this is an unsafe device and something has to be done.
I recorded the noise coming from the lighter on my smart phone.
justification: The lighter was actively leaking fuel, posing a high risk of fire and property damage.

incident_description: This is regarding the refill my six and a half inch Zippo Chrome Candle Lighter with butane.  The candlelighter was completely out of butane and in need of a full refill.  I have owned it for a few years without incident.  On the morning of December 26, 2016, (8:30 am), I stood over the kitchen sink with a flat wooden board at the bottom of the sink, covering the entire drain area---and proceeded to refill the candle lighter with butane.  This is something I have done many times over the years without any issues.  The lighter was refilling without any problems for the first ninety seconds, and was not yet refilled.  Then all of a sudden out of the blue, a huge 8 foot flame burst out.  How it occurred I do not know.  I did not have my hand (or fingers) near the igniter and am 100 % certain that I did not ignite the lighter.  There was nothing on or functioning in the kitchen except the main overhead light so the flame could not be explained by a microwave or [REDACTED] functioning.  As a result of this unexpected ignition, I received first and second degree burns which required immediate emergency room care, and then treatment at the St. Barnabas Burn Center..  I have blisters and may have permanent scarring all up and down my lower left arm.  I also have to continue to follow up with treatment at the Burn Center.  I have to apply Burn cream 2-3x daily and change the bandages often, not getting it wet in the shower.  Thus having to purchase a plastic arm protector to prevent it from getting wet.  I was told by the Emergency Room staff that I was very lucky.  Had I not been dressed wearing only my eyeglasses, t-shirt and shorts, the outcome may have been much more severe.  Had I not turned my body and pivoted, my face would definitely have been burned.  All the hair on my left arm was burned off, and the hair on the left side of my head was badly cinged.  Fortunately, there was no damage to my apartment and minimal damage to the immediate area where this occurred.  This was a very frightening experience.  I did contact Zippo Customer Service via email on December 26, 2016.  I never heard anything so I called Zippo Customer Care on December 27, 2016.  I asked to speak with a Manager and was told she was out until after the new year, but she would get back to me---and that my complaint had been received via email.  The Customer Service Representative I spoke with did not seem to take my issue very seriously, which really disgusted me.  In any case, I never received any information at any time regarding a product recall for this Zippo Candlelighter.  I want your agency to follow up and make sure this does not happen to anyone else.
justification: The incident resulted in significant injuries (first and second degree burns) and required immediate medical attention, but the likelihood of occurrence is rated as 'possible' due to the lack of clear cause and the user's history of safe refills.

incident_description:
A while back I purchased several Blitz Enviro-Flo Spouts for plastic gasoline containers from Walmart but I believe they are marketed through several other stores as well.  On the label they state they are a ÃÂSpill-Proof SystemÃÂ.  I recently noticed a can I have with gasoline was open and the spout and valve were laying on the ground yet the screw remained on the can and  was tight around the gas can.  The valve apparently just fell off while sitting on the floor of my garage.   There appears to be a serious design flaw in these spouts and when the spout fails, it can fall on the ground like mine did when no one is around, it can fall off if someone bumps the can or  if it was lightly bumped in the trunk of a car, or it could easily break when pouring gas since quite a bit of pressure is required to depress the valve to allow gasoline to flow.  The design flaw is associated with 6 very small plastic tabs that hold the spout together.  When the plastic deteriorates or fatigues, presumably due to aging or light, the plastic tabs can break off, and the spout separates from the can leaving an opening that is about 1.5ÃÂ across.
    Both the spout and the screw ring are very sturdy. The design flaw is in how the spout and the screw ring are held together.   They are coupled with a little piece of plastic that has 6 very small plastic tabs and in my case, two of the tabs failed and the spout fell off of the can.  The tabs are about the size of a flat wooden toothpick.  Prior to failing, the spout appears to be very strong and it is not apparent that this design flaw is present.  In my case, the  spout has probably been used only a few times so the wear on the product should have been negligable.  
    Should you have any interest, I can send the defective parts or pictures of the problem.  I am approaching you because I believe this design flaw is a problem waiting to occur with potentially devastating consequences.   Fortunately I found the problem without having a spill or a fire.   Although I am not a structural or safety engineer so am not qualified to give a professional opinion on this defect at this time, I am an electrical engineer and am keenly aware of public safety concerns and the importance of avoiding any designs or introducing any products  that are an inherent risk to the safety of the public.
justification: Although no incident occurred, the design flaw could lead to gasoline spills, posing a fire risk and potential injuries.

I have reviewed many reports of these cans being dangerous, dysfunctional, and broken online, most strongly on Amazon, I believe these products should be pulled from the market.

When the can is heated by exposure to the sun or even normal summer temperatures and then cooled in the evening, the can implodes, causing severe distortion of the sides of the can. incident_description: I purchased a Blue Rhino brand propane tank from my local Walmart. I connected this tank to my gas grill and when I opened the tank valve I heard gas leaking out from the connection point with my grill.  I reconnected the tank several times to insure it was properly connected but each time I opened the tank valve gas leaked from the connection. I removed the tank from the grill and inspected the valve. I found that the O ring inside the tank valve was missing. I returned the tank to the point of purchase and spoke with the store manager. I was given a replacement propane tank and the store manager and I inspected the valve to check for the O ring only to find that this tank too was missing the O ring. Without the O ring a seal is not made and gas leaks out potentially causing a fire/explosion hazard and injury if the user does not check for leaks prior to lighting the gas stove.

incident_description:
I purchased a Blue Rhino (Ferrellgas company) 20 pound propane tank which was missing the o ring inside the valve. The missing o ring caused the propane to leak which I consider very dangerous.  I contacted Ferrellgas via e mail and sent them the product code they requested along with photos of the tank and valve with no o ring.   Their response was, the code does not match up with their records.    According to the stamp on the tank it was recertified in Jan 2015. I bought the tank about 6 months ago and kept the tank stored inside.   I believe the certification is good for five years.  When I went to have it refilled, the technician said the "gas keeps blowing back". That's when he saw the o ring was totally gone.   I took the tank to a different  local propane supplier that verified the missing O ring.     
Blue Rhino seemed uninterested in the problem and would not acknowledge the tank may have passed their inspection without the o ring being installed.   The response from them was, "the rubber o ring could have dissolved over time, ect."
  I have never heard of an o ring "dissolving" and  was not pleased with the answer of the code I sent them "not matching their records".    I hope there are not other tanks out there with this defect.  Someone could get hurt if the leaking gas were to explode. 
Please pass this on or let others know of a possible danger.  I still have the tank, along with photos of the valve with missing  o ring if you are interested.  Thank you
justification: Although no injury occurred, the propane leak due to the missing O-ring poses a significant risk of explosion, making it an incident with high likelihood.

This is an addendum to the report referenced above, related to a severe gasoline storage container hazard: 

In approximately September, 2013 the caller purchased four 5-gallon plastic gasoline storage containers, manufactured by Blitz U.S.A. These were filled with automotive gasoline and stored in a sheltered location inside their garage. 

On or about July 15 of this year, he began to notice an odor of gasoline in the garage. It turned out that one of the four containers had a split along the line where the mold opens in the molding process used in manufacture. He poured the remaining gasoline into another container and left the leaking container in an outside location, with its cap removed, so that any remaining gasoline could evaporate. 

Then, on August 2, at which time they were away from home, he received a telephone call from a neighbor who had entered their garage. He reported that he had found a puddle of gasoline on the garage floor, over a fairly wide area -extending under the caller's car and flowing into a floor drain. The source was not one - but two - of the remaining 5-gallon containers which had split open. Obviously they were extremely fortunate that this did not result in an explosion or fire. 

The caller will now relate details about these storage containers. As it happens, he has a number of years' experience in the design and manufacture of molded plastic parts used in medical instruments. This experience includes dealing with the phenomenon of stress-cracking of products molded from high density polyethylene (HDPE). 

The containers are molded of red plastic which to the caller had the appearance of HDPE. However, he was not able to find anything on the container which identified the type of plastic. He was reassured by the Underwriters Laboratories symbol on the side, and the implication that the product was U.L. approved. The containers were manufactured by Blitz U.S.A. (which he understand went through bankruptcy several years ago - circa 2009 - because of product liability unrelated to failures of the molded container). 

The caller is enclosing 5 photographs of the container that failed first: 

Photo 1 - Shows the entire container, the manufacturer's emblem, and the U.L. emblem 

Photo 2 - Shows the lower handle area, with arrows indicating the location of the crack which caused leakage 

Photo 3 -Shows one side of the container, with legend identifying the manufacturer as Blitz U.S.A. Inc., of Miami, OK. Also shown is the model number: 31733 

Photo 4 -Shows the side opposite that of Photo 3 -the same side shown in Photo 1 but showing greater detail 

Photo 5 -Shows the bottom of the container, with a pair of time stamps 

The caller is retaining all 4 of the containers, should anyone have a need for further information which could be obtained by examining them. 

Since these failures occurred, the caller has visited their local Lowe's and Home Depot stores to obtain replacements. Lowe's had only a single metallic container available - all the rest were plastic and he was told by the manager that they were supplied by Blitz. Examining these containers, in various sizes, each one did have lettering which identified the plastic as HDPE. 

Stress cracking is a very well-known phenomenon which, to my knowledge, occurs only with HDPE. It is related to the semi-crystalline structure of HDPE, and occurs at the interface between microscopic crystal boundaries. It's very treacherous since it occurs with a tensile force on the plastic which causes far less than the 'yield stress' which will reproducibly cause stretching and failure on bench testing of strength. To cause this cracking, however, the tensile force must be applied for a long time. (In the case of my containers, it required about 3 years!) Typically it will take place where there is a 'stress riser' such as at a parting line which results from the molding process. It was at a parting line (along 
the inside of the handle) that failure occurred in the 3 of my containers which failed. 

Very unfortunately, it is extremely challenging - perhaps totally impossible - to evaluate products molded of HDPE for the possibility of delayed stress failure. This is because of the highly variable time required for failure, the variable effects of stress, the variable effects of storage conditions (temperature especially), and the variable effects of small differences in molding especially at a parting line where tool wear will result in changes over time. Further, depending on the molding process, there can be built-in residual stress which will result in eventual stress cracking without any additional stress being applied due to the weight of what is being stored (the weight of 5 gallons of gasoline is about 30 pounds). 

Following this container failure, the caller accessed the CPSC database, looking to see whether there are other reports of similar failures. In doing this, he found Report No. 20121018-70583-2147462751. This report describes failure of a Blitz fuel container (described as 'splitting') which occurred in 2012. It reportedly occurred 3 years after its purchase. Model number of the container was [REDACTED]. 

Gasoline will not attack HDPE. And, HDPE is inexpensive compared to many other plastics which could be used to store gasoline. However, because of its liability for stress-cracking. it should never be considered to be an appropriate or safe material for containers used to store gasoline or other hazardous liquids. 

It seems imperative, given the mission of the CPSC, to advise the public of the extreme danger of storing gasoline in containers molded of HDPE. Consideration could perhaps be given to advising that very short-term storage is less dangerous, given the process by which stress-cracking occurs. 

Obviously, there would be financial fall-out from such an action, but the possibility for tragic consequences from the use of such container would have to take strong priority. After talking with a local fire department official, it seems highly likely that there have indeed been a number of fires caused by such containers, without the cause being identifiable. 

Feel free to contact me if you judge that there might be any further useful information which I could provide. 

Very truly yours, 
[REDACTED]
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a significant fire hazard due to gasoline leaks from multiple containers, posing a high likelihood of future occurrences.
