The caller states that over time when the gasoline expands the seam breaks apart allowing gasoline to leak out of them 

He said he believes that these gas cans were manufactured of high density polyethylene which has a known propensity for stress cracking. 

He is reporting this occurrence after this happened to the first of 4 containers in his garage he has retained all of the containers. mid July 2016.

He then went on a vacation and received a call from his neighbor August 2nd, 2016 who informed him that two additional containers identical to the first one had split and gasoline was spilled under his car in his garage from these containers.

He said this needs to be reported as a fire hazard because other consumers may also have these gas cans in their possession.

there are no injuries being reported

He cannot contact the manufacturer, they are no longer in business


This is an addendum to the report referenced above, related to a severe gasoline storage container hazard:

In approximately September, 2013 the caller purchased four 5-gallon plastic gasoline storage containers, manufactured by Blitz U.S.A.  These were filled with automotive gasoline and stored in a sheltered location inside their garage.

On or about July 15 of this year, he began to notice an odor of gasoline in the garage.  It turned out that one of the four containers had a split along the line where the mold opens in the molding process used in manufacture.   He poured the remaining gasoline into another container and left the leaking container in an outside location, with its cap removed, so that any remaining gasoline could evaporate.

Then, on August 2, at which time they were away from home, he received a telephone call from a neighbor who had entered their garage. He reported that he had found a puddle of gasoline on the garage floor, over a fairly wide area -extending under the caller's car and flowing into a floor drain. The source was not one - but two - of the remaining 5-gallon containers which had split open. Obviously they were extremely fortunate that this did not result in an explosion or fire.

The caller will now relate details about these storage containers.  As it happens, he has a number of years' experience in the design and manufacture of molded plastic parts used in medical instruments.  This experience includes dealing with the phenomenon of stress-cracking of products molded from high density polyethylene (HDPE).

The containers are molded of red plastic which to the caller had the appearance of HDPE.   However, he was not able to find anything on the container which identified the type of plastic. He was reassured by the Underwriters Laboratories symbol on the side, and the implication that the product was U.L. approved. The containers were manufactured by Blitz U.S.A. (which he understand went through bankruptcy several years ago - circa 2009 - because of product liability unrelated to failures of the molded container).

The caller is enclosing 5 photographs of the container that failed first:

Photo 1  - Shows the entire container, the manufacturer's emblem, and the U.L. emblem

Photo 2 - Shows the lower handle area, with arrows indicating the location of the crack which caused leakage

Photo 3  -Shows one side of the container, with legend identifying the manufacturer as Blitz U.S.A. Inc., of Miami, OK.   Also shown is the model number: 31733

Photo 4  -Shows the side opposite that of Photo 3 -the same side shown in Photo 1 but showing greater detail

Photo 5 -Shows the bottom of the container, with a pair of time stamps

The caller is retaining all 4 of the containers, should anyone have a need for further information which could be obtained by examining them.

Since these failures occurred, the caller has visited their local Lowe's and Home  Depot stores to obtain replacements.  Lowe's had only a single metallic container available - all the rest were plastic and he was told by the manager that they were supplied by Blitz. Examining these containers, in various sizes, each one did have lettering which identified the plastic as HDPE.

Stress cracking is a very well-known phenomenon which, to my knowledge, occurs only with HDPE. It is related to the semi-crystalline structure of HDPE, and occurs at the interface between microscopic crystal boundaries.  It's very treacherous since it occurs with a tensile force on the plastic which causes far less than the 'yield stress' which will reproducibly cause stretching and failure on bench testing of strength.   To cause this cracking, however, the tensile force must be applied for a long time. (In the case of my containers, it required about 3 years!)  Typically it will take place where there is a 'stress riser' such as at a parting line which results from the molding process.  It was at a parting line (along
the inside of the handle) that failure occurred in the 3 of my containers which failed.

Very unfortunately, it is extremely challenging - perhaps totally impossible - to evaluate products molded of HDPE for the possibility of delayed stress failure. This is because of the highly variable time required for failure, the variable effects of stress, the variable effects of storage conditions (temperature especially), and the variable effects of small differences in molding especially at a parting line where tool wear will result in changes over time.  Further, depending on the molding process, there can be built-in residual stress which will result in eventual stress cracking without any additional stress being applied due to the weight of what is being stored (the weight of 5 gallons of gasoline is about 30 pounds).

Following this container failure, the caller accessed the CPSC database, looking to see whether there are other reports of similar failures. In doing this, he found Report No. 20121018-70583-2147462751. This report describes failure of a Blitz fuel container (described as 'splitting') which occurred in 2012.  It reportedly occurred 3 years after its purchase. Model number of the container was [REDACTED].

Gasoline will not attack HDPE.  And, HDPE is inexpensive compared to many other plastics which could be used to store gasoline.  However, because of its liability for stress-cracking. it should never be considered to be an appropriate or safe material for containers used to store gasoline or other hazardous liquids.

It seems imperative, given the mission of the CPSC, to advise the public of the extreme danger of storing gasoline in containers molded of HDPE.  Consideration could perhaps be given to advising that very short-term storage is less dangerous, given the process by which stress-cracking occurs.

Obviously, there would be financial fall-out from such an action, but the possibility for tragic consequences from the use of such container would have to take strong priority.   After talking with a local fire department official, it seems highly likely that there have indeed been a number of fires caused by such containers, without the cause being identifiable.

Feel free to contact me if you judge that there might be any further useful information which I could provide.

Very truly yours,
[REDACTED]
justification: Although no injuries were reported, the incident involved a significant fire hazard due to gasoline leaks from multiple containers, posing a high likelihood of future incidents.

incident_description:
The consumer had about five of the lighters that exploded at different times without any warning. One was under his laptop, the other four were lying  on the desk.  The products were not exposed to direct sunlight per the consumer.

No injuries.
justification: Multiple lighters exploding without warning indicates a high likelihood of future incidents.

incident_description:
I have three 5gallon metal gas cans. I used to have to replace the nozzles periodically. Now, because off new regulations, I can't but these replacement nozzles. Because of this, I was forced to purchase new plastic ventless cans. The nozzle on these cans require 3 hand to dispense gas from the can. 
This is the most dangerous thing that I have do right now in my life. The threads on the plastic cans are poorly designed and have separated from the can several times as I was filling my lawnmower spilling gas all over the lawnmower. 

I can't b the only person complaining about this. What is being done to correct this stupidity? How many people have to injured or killed before this nonsense is corrected?
justification: The poorly designed threads on the plastic cans pose a high likelihood of injury due to the risk of separation while filling, as evidenced by the incident described.

incident_description: I keep a lighter in my car, stored in the ashtray. On 4/19/2016, as soon as I opened the car door, there was loud pop, some smoke and slight sulfur smell. The Scripto lighter, previously in the ashtray, was in pieces on the passenger side floor, and the metal top piece was hot and on the passenger seat. No injuries or damage, but small plastic pieces were scattered around the front of the car.
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries or damage, but the occurrence of the lighter exploding was possible given its improper storage in the car.

incident_description: My 11 year old son was holding a TNT brand California Candle firework.  It is a large sparkler-type hand held firework.  He was using it per the instructions written on the firework.  Suddenly, the back end (the side he was holding) exploded.  He suffered pain in his ears and burns on his forearm, along with emotional trauma.
justification: The firework exploded unexpectedly in his hand, causing burns and pain, despite following instructions.

incident_description: We were lighting the fireworks and they were faulty. Rather than shooting up in the air, they malfunctioned and the fireworks shot sideways and into the spectators. The product names were "Charger" and "[REDACTED]". Both products are distributed by "World Class Fireworks". Several spectators were injured - none appeared to be serious.
justification: Several spectators were injured due to faulty fireworks malfunctioning and shooting sideways.

incident_description:
faulty fuel ignition/disbursement design.  there is no 'Warning" on the BIC mini lighters to indicate the inconsistent, and dangerously high flame when they are new;  there either needs to be a 'regulator' for the amount/flame size OR, they should make the mini with an adjustable flame.

I only smoke outdoors.  while using any new BIC Mini lighter, the flame is huge and uncontrollable; if even the slightest breeze blows by, the flame will burn fingers/knuckles/fingernails & nose/nose hairs.  If I had long hair & wore it down. I would NOT even use this lighter.  In addition, the 'warning' says avoid temps of 120 --  all it takes is the lighter being in a pocket at 75 degrees and the flame reaches a very dangerous height.

My complaint/concerns addressed directly to BIC resulted in a 'coupon'.
justification: The inconsistent, high flame poses a high risk of burns to fingers, knuckles, and facial hair, especially in outdoor conditions.

incident_description:
The new gasoline storage cans for home-owner use now have check valves to prevent the gasoline from pouring out until the spout is pressed inward on the gas tank (such as on a lawn mower). This new safety feature is supposed to prevent the accidental spilling of the gasoline. However, it actually creates a greater safety hazard. If the gasoline storage container gets warm, and you then depress the spout while filling your lawnmower, the pressure in the gas can causes the gasoline to blow out all over the lawnmower. If the lawnmower is hot, there is a fire and explosion hazard. These new gas cans need a vent to release the pressure before you tip over the container and press in the nozzle. 

The consumer is reporting all gas cans that have this new "safety" feature. The consumer states the heat creates the pressure and an incident is more likely to occur during the summer than during the colder seasons.

The consumer has created a vent hole to prevent another incident with his gas can.
justification: The new design increases the likelihood of an incident due to pressure buildup, potentially leading to a fire or explosion.

incident_description:
I was preparing to refuel my lawn mower using a Justrite, Type2, 2 Gallon Safety Can containing gasoline. The can was approximately 20 percent full and about 2 years old.

The lawn mower was cool.
The safety can was in my garage, not in direct sunlight, prior to filling.
Temperature in the garage was 90 F. Humidity was 60 %.

I inserted the flexible nozzle into the gas tank and squeezed the silver gas release handle.  A large amount of air/ gas vapor drove the gasoline at a high velocity into the gas tank.  The gasoline splashed back approximately 3 feet into my eyes, nose and mouth.

The can has been emptied and is in my possession.

The company and Consumer Reports have been notified.
justification: Gasoline splashed back into eyes, nose, and mouth causing potential injury.

incident_description:
Product: WeatherRite Outdoor double-mantle propane gas lantern (600 candlepower). It uses standard camping propane tanks.
Age: about 10 years old.
Incident: On May 19, 2016 after using this lantern about 10-15 days/year for about ten years, it suddenly began to leak gas at the valve while operating. It happened In a state park, at an outdoor table, I noticed a change in the sound it made, and immediately smelled gas. Flames leapt from the valve. I blew them out , and turned off the lantern. I have not resumed using it.
Contact with company: On May 20, I contacted the company and sent photos of the lantern, including the instructions. Web search indicates that WeatherRite is now a brand of Alliance Sports Group
3025 N Great Southwest Pkwy, Grand Prairie, TX 75050, T 972-343-1001  www.nebotools.com
Action by company: As of May 28, I have not heard from the company
Recall: I did not see any recall on the CSPC website. However, the incident appears somewhat similar to the [REDACTED]. The lantern also is similar. 
[REDACTED]
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the lantern leaking gas and flames leaping from the valve pose a significant risk, making it an incident with potential for injury.

incident_description:
Using a Scripto foldable, refillable utility lighter to light the wood in my family fire pit, the lighter backflashed and burned my hand, arm and face.  It burned my lips, eyes, forehead; and singed off my facial hair and bangs.

The product was purchased in March 2016; and the incident happend on May1, 2016.  

I want this model recalled.
justification: The incident resulted in burns and singed hair, classifying it as an injury (severity level 3). The likelihood of occurrence is possible (3) given the common use of lighters and the potential for backflashing.

incident_description: Two cigarette lighters exploded. One exploded in my purse, the other one was in my jeans pocket and exploded while I was taking my jeans off to change.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the explosion of two cigarette lighters in close proximity to the body is a significant event, making it an incident with a possible occurrence likelihood.

incident_description:
(04/13/2106) The consumer stated that his  wife heard a loud explosion that came from near her granddaughters room. She went to investigate and saw that the lighter had exploded and pieces were scattered throughout the room. The lighter was located on a desk. It was not exposed to light or heat. No one was in the room when the lighter exploded.

No injuries.

The consumer added he attached 3 digital photos (poor quality) of the lighter, and lighter pieces and a candle that was broken by the lighter after it exploded.  The consumer also added all evidence have been retained and are available at [CPSC's] request.
justification: No injuries occurred despite the explosion, but the incident caused property damage.

incident_description:
The fuel dispensing nozzle of a Briggs & Stratton gas can does not prevent spillage of the fuel when in storage mode, even when the can if filled only to the fill line. When stored, the nozzel is inverted into the can, and it seems to siphon the fuel out of the can. Additionally, there is a cap that is supposed to fit over the open end of the inverted nozzle, but it cannot be secured, allowing fuel to spill.
The name of this product is Briggs & Stratton Self Venting Smart Fill Nozzle System.
This product is an immedite threat to anyone who uses it.
justification: The design flaw in the nozzle system makes fuel spillage likely, posing an immediate threat of property damage and potential injury.

incident_description: MK disposable lighter exploded in my wife's hands near her face severely injuring her hand and face.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injuries to the individual's hand and face, warranting a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is rated 3 as while not common, incidents involving disposable lighters exploding are possible.

incident_description: I was sitting on my bed when a lighter I had go from the smoke shop down the street just exploded.  It's a Quantum lighter and was brand new and it made a loud pop sound and had a piece of plastic that separated from the main body so the fluid leaked out all over my desk.
justification: The incident resulted in property damage but no injuries, and while it's possible for a lighter to malfunction, it's not a common occurrence.

incident_description:
The consumer had fuel stored in his container. The consumer stated that he was pouring fuel into his tractor that takes a large amount of fuel compared to lawn mower. The consumer stated that his container imploded because there was no air being transferred into the container.

The consumer contacted the firm in regards to the incident. They would not send him a replacement container. The consumer sent an e-mail with photos to the firm. They informed him that they will speak to their engineers and he would receive a letter from them.

The consumer stated that it has been few weeks and he has not heard from anyone.  

The consumer believes that this is a safety hazard because the can was full. The fuel could have shot out of the spout and spilled in surrounding area.
justification: While no injury occurred, the container implosion could have led to fuel spillage, posing a potential hazard.

incident_description: Char-broil live it up propane tank hose. model number 7184633.  I recently purchased this hose and it was leaking from the 20 lb tank connection.  I returned it to the place of purchase and exchanged it.  The second hose was leaking in the exact same place.  The pressed fitting on the rubber section of the hose.  I confirmed this with using soapy water on the connection.
justification: Leaking propane hose could lead to a fire or explosion, posing a significant risk.

incident_description: disposable cigarette lighter explode in shirt pocket.....made in China...Solar brand
justification: The incident resulted in no injuries, but the explosion of a disposable cigarette lighter in a shirt pocket could have caused property damage or minor burns.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that her son was watching TV and the cigarette lighter was laying on his bed. Her son heard a popping sound from the lighter. The consumer stated that the lighter exploded soon after the popping sound. 

The top part of the lighter blew off of the bottom part. The consumer has the bottom part of the lighter. The consumer threw away the other unused lighters.
 
The consumer stated that the explosion burned a hole in the mattress and the bed sheet. The consumer has photographs.
 
The consumer will be contacting the manufacturer regarding the incident.
justification: The lighter exploding caused property damage but no injuries, hence severity level 2.

incident_description: Firework was lit at the top wick and held at the bottom as directed on the package.  The top of the firework was pointed up and away from any observers.  After being lit for about 3 seconds, a fireball shot out of the bottom of the tube and directly into the waistband of my jeans.  The fireball burned through the pocket of my jeans and melted part of my iphone case and screen protector.  I was able to shake the fireball down the leg of my pants onto the grass. My husband sprayed me with a garden hose to stop the burning flame.  I immediately went inside to look at my injuries.  I had charred and burned flesh on my stomach and spots on my leg where the fireball traveled down. After cleaning the areas, I put ice on the injury and applied [REDACTED] and gauze.  The pain was bad and 3 days later, I went to my primary care provider for medical evaluation.  I was diagnosed with 3rd degree burns and prescribed [REDACTED] cream.  I had 2 follow up visits for this injury per my doctor's orders.  I still have a scar on my stomach approximately 2x3 inches that is red, uneven scar tissue.
justification: The incident resulted in third-degree burns, requiring medical attention, but did not result in death.

incident_description:
10/31/2015 - The consumer indicates the unit was sitting on concrete floor in a metal building. The consumer was working with a circular saw cutting through metal about twenty feet away from the can. The sparks caused by the circular saw were not reaching the can but because vapor must have been evaporating because when the consumer looked to the can he saw that it was on fire.

The consumer indicates that the imbalanced ratio to oxygen vapor level inside the can is what causes these fires and explosions, as well as the bad quality of the can; thankfully, his gasoline can was almost full.

11/02/2015 - The consumer contacted the manufacturer and explained what had happened. The representative informed the consumer that they could replace the spout. The representative was adamant to know what had actually happened. The consumer is not interested in the spout because they are not safe.

The consumer has no injuries nor previous incidents to report. The consumer believes this product poses a safety hazard.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a fire caused by sparks from a nearby circular saw, indicating a high likelihood of occurrence.

incident_description: I was attempting to light a cigarette and the J&D lighter exploded in my face causing 2nd degree burns to my nose, lips and right ear lobe.
justification: The incident resulted in significant injuries (2nd degree burns) and the likelihood of such an event occurring is possible given the common use of lighters.

incident_description: The product is a "Click n Flame" Wind Resistant butane lighter.  I had lite a candle with lighter and released the safety and trigger and placed it on the table.  I heard it still hissing faintly and picked it back up and noticed that it was stilling flaming.   Flame had not gone out when the trigger was released.
justification: The lighter continued to flame after the trigger was released, posing a fire hazard but no immediate injury was reported.

incident_description: While camping with the family, we were using a Coleman 2 Piece Propane Tree (Model No.2000005192) to connect my propane lantern to a standard 20lb propane tank. While using the lantern, the plastic "hand wheel" (as they call it on their website) that attaches the propane tree to the propane tank split in two and caused the propane tree to pivot where it connects to the tank, causing the lantern to come crashing down and break on the ground. Had I not been incredibly careful to keep it away from anything combustible, it could have easily started a fire. This was only the 3rd time I have used the propane tree and the plastic nut (or "hand wheel") was only hand tightened onto the propane tank per the instructions. I would guess that material expansion and contraction caused by the change in temperature caused the plastic to break. It was almost 90 degrees out and running the lantern caused the propane tank to get cold. I would consider this to be a very big safety flaw. That nut should clearly be made out of a material that can withstand these types of temperature fluctuations since it is not uncommon for people to use it during the summer and propane tanks will always get cold when being used.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a potential fire hazard due to a defective plastic nut on the propane tree, making it likely to recur.

incident_description:
Problem associated with Blitz EnviroFlo gasoline container. UPC code 44549 80010. Container had been filled a relatively small number of times; probably no more than 20.

Gasoline can plastic nozzle failed. It developed a crack which was not readily visible. During routine fill operation, gasoline leaked from the crack and onto hot engine parts. Gasoline was readily vaporized.
justification: Gasoline leak onto hot engine parts posed a high risk of ignition and injury.

incident_description: Smelled gas in interior of house.  Called gas company to insure it was not natural gas.  No leak found by gas company.  Traced leak to propane Fire Pit gas regulator seal (model number RA329, made by Ningbo Wanan).  Gas made it into interior of home because patio door was left open (screen door closed).  Air vented into house to remove gas.  Fortunately no damage or injury.
justification: Although no injury occurred, the incident involved a gas leak into the house, posing a potential hazard.

incident_description:
The consumer purchased butane fuel refill containers which are used to refill butane lighters. The consumer purchased 2 containers of the butane fuel and the consumer has filed a similar report.

On 9/10/15 the consumer used the product to refill his lighter and later in the day he began to have chest pains. The next day (9/11/15) the consumer states his chest pains were worse and he had difficulty moving and breathing. The consumer believes his chest pains are from exposure to the butane fuel.

The consumer plans to visit a physician.

On 9/14/15 the consumer contacted the vendor and expressed his safety concerns with the product. The consumer spoke with [REDACTED], the owner of the store. The consumer states [REDACTED] became upset and told the consumer that there is nothing wrong with the product. The consumer then contacted the Poison Control (800-222-1222) and was advised to go to the hospital. 

The consumer states he has been purchasing butane gas for years but this is the first time he purchased this particular product. The consumer believes this product poses a health hazard and should be recalled. 

The consumer used about 1/4 of the product. 

Did I See A Doctor, because of the reported exposure:

On 9/14/2015 after submitting the Butane exposure incident report to CPSC, I went directly to the Miami VA Hospital's emergency room in Miami, Florida, arriving at around 1:30 PM.  I was triaged and at 6:40 PM that day, admitted as an inpatient to the hospital.  While in the hospital, I was subjected to a battery of tests including cardio (also stress test), pulmonary and other tests to eliminate them as being the cause of the chest pains I experienced from the Butane exposure I reported.  All tests were normal or within normal and excepted ranges for my age and other factors.

The final analysis was, after nearly two days of around the clock testing and monitoring, that the cause of my chest pains, was likely as I initially reported, Butane Fuel.  I was released from the hospital on 9/16/2015 at around 5 PM.
justification: The consumer experienced severe chest pains and difficulty breathing after using the product, leading to hospitalization and diagnosis of butane exposure.

incident_description:
Purchased two 2-gallon plastic fuel containers from Walmart on Aug 5 at the Airway Heights, WA store.  Containers made by Specter Corp.  

Both containers leak fuel when trying to pour.  A rubber gasket is provided which came placed between the spout and the cap.  When tightened in this position the gasket slips out of place coming out between the spout and cap.  Tried putting the gasket between the spout and container but will not stay in place.  

Found that placing the gasket between the cap and spout there is a ridge on the spout with a small notch where a gasket could fit but the gasket provided is 2-3 time thicker than the notch so will not fit.

The leak is not a small leak but a fair size stream which creates very quickly a large fire hazard.  

Product needs to be recalled immediately as a extreme safety hazard.
justification: The significant fuel leak poses a high risk of fire, potentially leading to property damage and injuries.

incident_description: On July 4, 2015 my niece was lighting a YOYO metal sparkler and the flame shot backwards and sounded like a rocket  severely burning her hand. We saw a recall for this product on July 9, 2015 on a DFW news page on Facebook.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe burn, and the product was recalled shortly after, indicating a high likelihood of similar occurrences.

incident_description:
MSR Flammable Gas Canisters Leak.  Problem discovered before any injury could happen.    

   On July 8, 2014 I received from Mountain Gear a case of twenty four  MSR brand 8oz/227gram (net) canisters of an 80% isobutane-20% propane mix used as backpacking stove fuel.

-While testing my non-MSR stoves ([REDACTED] and [REDACTED] brands) for compatibility with the new MSR canister, using a bubble solution, I found that it leaked.  I tried another...leaked.  I tried 9 total.  All 9 leaked
.
-I found that there was a leak from the canister itself, NOT the connection between stove and can.  I was 90+% certain of this.

-On Saturday, 7/12/14, I called Mountain Gear, the retailer; DOT-Hazmat; and Cascade Designs, the parent company of MSR. 
   -There was a live operator at Mountain Gear.  I explained, and she said she'd try to get a note to other order takers to not sell/ship any more of this lot #.  I called again Sunday and was advised to ship it back for inspection, replacement or refund.
   -Left voice mail with DOT [1-800-467-4922].  [REDACTED] left a message on my machine on Monday, asking me to call again.
   -Left voice mail with Cascade Designs.  No calls or messages from them as of 5:37PM PST, Wednesday 7/16.

-To be 100% certain that the problem was wholly with the canister before pursuing this any further, I borrowed a friend's MSR brand backpacking stove. (It can be seen in the background in the full view picture.)  I tried the MSR stove on 3 canisters that I hadn't tried my own stoves on.  All 3 leaked from the same place.  I am now 100% sure the fault is entirely with the MSR product, and not a brand incompatibility issue. 
  
-Total # of canisters tested:  12.  All leaked.  Most tested canisters were from top layer in case, but at least 4 were tested from bottom layer.  Two in each layer were totally "internal", not in contact with sides of carton.  All four of these were among those tested.

Details about leak:
   -Canisters leak only from under the outer ring of the canister valve. (see picture 0025)  The outer ring is composed of two layers of metal pressed together and curving around to form a lip.
   -One of my stoves allowed me to see the gas connection between stove and canister while the stove was fully screwed on.  I poured bubble mixture in there, and no bubbles formed.
   -Canisters start to leak only when stove is attached.
   -Leakage is slow.
   -No flare-ups noted from leaking area while stove was fired up, but I only fired up the stoves on ~4 of the MSR canisters, and didn't run them more than a minute.
   -After stove is detached, bubbles continue to form for 10-30 seconds, depending on canister.
  -When I tested my new stoves on 2 canisters I already had at home, ([REDACTED] and [REDACTED] brands), NEITHER LEAKED.   I'm now 110% sure the problem is entirely with the MSR cannister!

Thoughts:
-One hazard is if someone doesn't detach the stove from the can, and puts it in their pack, tent, car trunk, gear bin, or closet.  A dangerous amount of gas could build up then.  
-If the quality of manufacturing gets worse, or already is worse in other lot #'s, the danger could increase. 

What I've done about this so far:
  I considered returning the product to Mountain Gear, as they suggested.  But I thought this could be a serious problem, or eventually turn into a serious problem if the manufacturer slipped up even worse.  Cascade Designs didn't reply to my first phone call, which suggested to me that they didn't care enough about this.  So I decided to hold onto the product and contact the Dep't of Transportation.  On July 16, 2014 I sent a detailed e-mail with photos to [REDACTED] at DOT, HazMat division.  He was very interested, but as it turns out, it doesn't seem to be a transportation hazard, so I don't think his office has pursued it.  I called Cascade Designs again and forwarded the same e-mail to [REDACTED] [Customer Service rep] there around 7/29/14.   They asked for more info on 8/3, which I promptly sent.  On 8/27 I emailed [REDACTED], asking what they'd found out so far.  His reply included this very frustrating phrase: "we are now going continue on with the information that we have, and build on it without further input or communication outside Cascade Designs."   True to his word, they haven't tried to communicate with me!  I still have most of the e-mails.  PLEASE convince them to communicate with you!  [REDACTED], DOT, suggested I report this to your agency.  But by then I was too tired and frustrated with the whole affair to contact anyone else.  Recently I've been thinking "I really need to get this ball rolling again".  Minutes before starting on this report form (which has disappeared 2x so far!) I e-mailed [REDACTED] at CD to ask for a progress report and advice on what to do with the fuel.   But I will hold onto it for you.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the incident involved a significant safety hazard with multiple canisters leaking flammable gas, making it likely to cause injury if not addressed.

incident_description: Lit a Yo Yo sparkler and the whole sparkler erupted into a ball of flame and shot down into the hand holding the sparkler.  This happened in less than a second.  Dropped sparkler immediately.  Serious burns to the hand.  Went to the E.R. for treatment.
justification: The sparkler's unexpected and rapid transformation into a ball of flame resulted in serious burns, indicating a high likelihood of similar occurrences.

incident_description: I was lighting yoyo sparklers.  I was holding 4 sparklers in my left hand and when they light they completely ignited instead of slowly burning. I now have 2/3 degree burns in my left hand.
justification: The incident resulted in significant burns, but not life-threatening, and the likelihood of such an event occurring is possible given the handling of multiple sparklers.

incident_description:
I am the Fire Marshal for the Commack Fire Department in New York. I was recently on an inspection in a restaurant, public assembly, when the manager showed me a bag full of fireworks fountains he purchased on-line. Nowhere on the package does it say fireworks and it shows a graphic of a cake with these items on it shooting out sparks. The name on the package of the item is called "Birthday Candles". It does in extremely small print on the back where a staple was through the package to hold it together that it was for outdoor use. However when you go to the website selling these fountains and on the package itself, they're being marketed as birthday candles. When I inquired about how and where this gentleman obtained them he said we went to a website called [REDACTED], put in his credit card and they shipped them to him no questions asked.
So I tested these "candles" and they're not even close to being a candle. when lit, they emit a flame jet approximately ten inches high and shoot sparks of what I would guess is magnesium flakes about 16 inches high. They have a short plastic pin on the bottom of them that is supposed to go into the cake, its only about a half inch long and will very easily tip over. The flame ignited anything flammable that I put within 12 inches of it. 
This is no birthday cake candle or sparkler, this is a fireworks fountain that brings back memories of the pyrotechnic "gerbs" used in the Station Night Club fire back in 2002 but just on a smaller scale. These items are dangerous and its not a matter of if, but rather, when they're going to be the cause of a multi-fatality fire..
justification: These items are marketed as harmless birthday candles but are in fact dangerous fireworks fountains that can cause serious fires and injuries, as demonstrated by the Fire Marshal's test.

incident_description:

incident_description:
I have always had concern about the design of the spout on this gas can.  Nearly every time I use it I end up with a mess of gas on either the lawn mower or my hands, and based on the reviews I now see on Amazon for this product I am not alone.  It is difficult to use and error prone, which is disturbing considering it is meant to store and use a dangerous chemical like gasoline.

This can appears to be designed for environmental purposes, so that vapors cannot escape.  As such the can is airtight, and seems to have no method of venting other than manually pressing in the spout to open it.  Because of this airtight nature temperature changes can cause a great deal of pressure build up in the can.  I normally vent the can outside in a safe direction, but even so it seems dangerous when sometimes gas can spray out of the can due to the extreme pressure.  On 6/13/15 I did not take this step, and attempted to fill my lawn mower tank using the way provided in the instructions, which is to unlock the spout, set the catch on the lip of the gas fill hole of the mower, and press down.  Because of the pressure the gas came out extremely quickly, instantly overflowing the tank and getting all over the mower.  I set the can back in my garage next to the wall, and proceeded to clean up the mower.  After getting it clean I thought I should release any little bit of remaining pressure in the can by pulling down on the spout to open it up.  I assumed most of the pressure had been released in the first incident.  Unfortunately there was still a lot of pressure in the can, as well as a piece of curved plastic next to my garage wall.  The spray of gasoline from the can hit the plastic and was redirected back into my face.  After washing and flushing my eyes, face, and basically entire head for about 20 minutes I headed to the ER.  They found a 2mm chemical burn in my left eye and two separate 2mm burns in my right eye, and proceeded to further flushed my eyes using saline.

I believe this can should be recalled.  It is unthinkable that such a dangerous and difficult to use product is on the market, not just for me but scores of other people.  I have been using gas cans to fill lawn mowers for over 30 years and have never had any experience like this.  In the best case a person will occasionally get gas on their hands while using this product, which is bad enough.  People in the area of the can are obviously in danger of being sprayed under certain circumstances.  I even have concerns about the can bursting due to the pressure, as I have at times seen it swell considerably on hot days.
justification: User experienced chemical burns in both eyes due to unexpected high pressure release from the gas can, indicating a likely occurrence.

incident_description: On Saturday, April 18, 2015, consumer was prepared to grill on his back deck.  He used Frontier brand EcoStart Natural Lighter Fuel Gel ("EcoStart"), with charcoal.  He prepared the grill and placed the bottle of Ecostart to the left of the grill.  He then lit the charcoal with a lighter.  He picked the bottle of EcoStart up to move it back to storage and as he did, the bottle started to whistle and before he could react, the bottle of EcoStart exploded.  The burning fuel gel was ejected all over his upper body.  He attempted to extinguish the flames with blankets and pillows, and his partner tried pouring liquids on him.  It was several minutes before the flames were extinguished, and not before spreading to some additional objects, including his pants.  He was rushed to the hospital where the doctors at the Burn Center determined that he had suffered second and third-degree burns to at least 15% of his total body.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns to 15% of the victim's body, and the likelihood of such an event occurring given the actions taken is high.

incident_description:

incident_description:
I just purchased a Briggs & Stratton Smart Fill Fuel Filling System 2 Gallon CARB G-10-010 manufactured by the Plastics Group (www.theplatsicsgroup.net) at a local Walmart (Fairfax, VA) and discovered a defect that appears to be common among all of that model and the other models that use the same nozzle system.

The container is sold with the nozzle mechanism inserted inside leaving it to the purchaser to remove the mechanism and install it for use.  Unfortunately the mechanism is inserted in a such a way that upon removing it the mechanism cap ÃÂ that is the nozzle cap ÃÂ does not fit through the container opening.  The nozzle assembly can be removed but the nozzle cap remains inside the container.  As that nozzle cap is slightly larger than the container opening, upon positioning the container for pouring fuel that cap lodges itself in the opening, closing it and preventing the fuel from being poured.  This is in turn can lead to dangerous situations in which fuel is spilled in the process of trying to dislodge the cap. 

I urge you to take action in order to correct this defect and recall the affected products.
justification: The defect can lead to fuel spills, posing a risk of fire or injury.

justification: Gasoline splash and skin contact resulted in irritation and itching, classifying as an injury.

incident_description:
Ingestion date: 16/09/14
16 month old male, previously healthy, with witnessed ingestion of Tiki Torch (R) Fuel from canister,also some spilled on clothing. Within 1 hour he was lethargic and had difficulty breathing with continued coughing, with questionable apnea at home, treated by rescue breathing by mother. He was then transported to the local emergency department.

Initial emergency x-ray appeared normal; however, subsequent decompensation to complete white out occurred on the second image. He was then intubated and transferred to a tertiary care facility  and admitted to a pediatric ICU with toxicology bedside consultation. Upon admission he was  transitioned to an oscillator and developed bilateral pneumothoraces after 1 week with further progression which required placement of bilateral chest tubes. He continued to have ongoing issues with desaturation and 2 PRBC transfusions for oxygenation purposes were administered.

Broad spectrum antibiotics and antifungal therapy were provided over the course of admission for treatment of pneumonia. Additionally, the patient developed tolerance/dependence to opioids (fentanyl and morphine) and benzodiazepines (midazolam) during ventilation and required taper for withdrawal prevention with methadone, clonidine, and lorazepam.

Outcomes: 
Chronic lung disease secondary to prolonged respiratory failure/chemical pneumonitis with prescription for budesonide, continued aspiration risk with swallowing issues which required restriction to thickened fluid diet and famotidine.

Discharge date from hospital: 24/12/2014
justification: The child developed severe respiratory distress, pneumothoraces, and required ICU admission, indicating a significant injury (severity level 3). The detailed description and multiple occurrences of similar incidents in the dataset make this likely (occurrence likelihood 4).

incident_description: The consumer was at a Fourth of July celebration on July 4, 2013.   As part of the holiday celebrations, a 6 shot, cake-style consumer firework was set off.  The firework was set on a flat, level surface and lit by the consumer, at which point he backed away from the firework.  The firework then misfired, firing a shot laterally from the packaging hitting the consumer in his face, rather than firing vertically up into the air. The firework name was "Bottoms Up" and contained a trademarked "Boomer" logo, which was registered by Jake's Fireworks, Inc.  The firework was manufactured in China and imported by Jake's Fireworks, Inc.

incident_description:
On June 19th, my daughter and I were outside, sitting on a couch while reading next to our fire pit. We bought the fire pit at our local garden store (similar ones are available in numerous locations, including Restoration Hardware) and it uses bio-fuel. The label on this product reads, "Co-Z Fire: Pure, Safe, Eco-Friendly Bio-ethanol Fireplace Fuel" and we opted for this product since it burns clean (no unhealthy smoke) and seemed "safe". When the flame appeared to be extinguished, my husband added more of the pourable fuel to the dish. Within an instance, the fire appeared to explode outward in an enormous fireball, landing on my daughter's legs. We both jumped on top of her to extinguish the flames but they were relentless in a way that we've never seen. She suffered horrific 2nd and 3rd degree burns over 75% of her legs and spent 2 weeks at St. Francis' Bothin Burn center. 

From what I've read, she was fortunate. The injuries resulting from similar bio-fuel accidents can be significantly worse and cause irreparable damage and death. It also appears that this product has not been adequately tested and is somewhat unregulated due to its classification as a "decorative fire pot." The labeling is completely misleading -- this product is far from "safe". 

We urge you to move forward with a ban on bio-fuel and are quite surprised and outraged that it has taken the CPSC as long as it has to address this ongoing issue. Burns from bio-fuel accidents are happening at an alarming rate and are entirely avoidable. Please take action before additional people (and children!) suffer at the expense of this product category that shouldn't exist.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns (2nd and 3rd degree) over 75% of the daughter's legs, and similar incidents are happening frequently due to inadequate testing and misleading labeling of bio-fuel products.

incident_description:
I just purchased Home Depot's advertised Memorial Day red/white/blue bamboo torch 6-pack special.  I planted each in the ground and the unscrewed the cap of each and used a funnel to add new name-brand torch fuel from a sealed container.  Just opening each proofed to be a challenge, either thanks to the cheap metal being warped or the paint acting as a sealant, but I was eventually able to open and fill each and ready to light.  

I ensured that I wiped each one down thoroughly before lighting to ensure there was no spilled fuel, and also gathered together the frayed ends of each wick and poked down until only a quarter to half-inch of wick was exposed, as I had learned from my previous torches that this helps control the flame size.  But by the time I lit the last one, I looked back and realized that the entire fuel canister of the first torch was engulfed, and the second well on its way to doing the same.  

I quickly ran over to blow out the torch, but the flame was too large to extinguish by blowing it out.  Fortunately I had a power blower on hand that I quickly cranked up and pointed at the torch (with throttle at idle).  Just this amount of wind was enough to break the top support band that holds the fuel canister in place between the vertical prongs, and sent the now extinguished canister rolling across the lawn.  Similar result followed with the second and third torch which had become engulfed in flame as well, and finally the fourth which was just starting to get out of control.  

The problem seemed to be that too much fuel was being wicked up from the container, but I discovered once they cooled that they were not well sealed, and were all leaking from around the lid and from each seam at the top and bottom.  Thankfully it wasn't too windy and no alcohol had been consumed, otherwise this could have ended much differently.
justification: While no injuries occurred, the incident involved multiple torches catching fire simultaneously, posing a significant risk of property damage and potential injury.

I opened the envelope containing the product which came with a sheet of instructions. There was no product name or serial numbers on the product nor any manufacturing data. I read the instructions and followed them precisely. As I attempted to light the product, fuel spilled from the product reservoir and the spark from lighting the match ignited the fuel which had also spilled on my hand. Flames appeared on my left hand and fingers. I dropped the product to extinguish the flames on my hand. After the flames on my hand were extingquished I noticed that the lighter, that had been thrown down was engulfed in flames. I tried stamping the fire out with my foot but it would not extinguish. I then fetched a cup of water from a nearby sink and poured the water on the product which finally extinguished. The plastic on the product had melted to the point that the product was no longer usable. I sustained some minor first degree burns on my left hand and fingers.
justification: The product's design flaw caused fuel to spill, leading to minor burns, hence severity level 3. The detailed instructions and common match-lighting action make this occurrence likely.

incident_description:
Newly purchased gasoline container is inherently unsafe as it will always result in gasoline spills until it is fully configured. 

Wife purchased a "Spillproof" 1 gallon gasoline container from Midwest container corporation. 
The unit was filled with Gasoline and the cap tightened normally. On the way home, the unit tipped over (due to it's tall square design, this is almost unavoidable), and spilled gasoline all over the inside of the trunk. Upon inspection, there is no gasket or seal between the cap and the container, which allows fuel to leak out and create a hazard. The attached spout actually contains the gasket, and when properly inserted, will help to avoid spills, but this is not the way the product is sold. The seller does not attach the spout to the can, but leaves it separate. 
To attach the spout, the cap's center must be punched out, and the spout inserted through the cap, and then tightened to the can. 

The design of the can seems to be such that the spout is spill resistant. But as noted above, the container is taller than it is wide, is square, and the spout is not inserted into the cap when sold. All of these things serve to defeat the spill resistant nature of the design.
justification: The incident resulted in a spill but no injuries, and the likelihood of occurrence is high due to the product's design and the seller's instructions.

incident_description:
Scepter 18.8L/5Gal Eco plastic gas can.  UPC=063923975435

The gas cans were use to fill a boat and lawn mower fuel tank.  The four gas cans were purchased from the Jupiter, Florida Walmart on Indiantown Road approximately two months ago.  Each gas can was used approximately six times.

After a few uses of transferring fuel from the gas can to the boat and lawn mower, a hazardous situation was created when fuel leaked from between the gas can and spout.  Some of the fuel ran down the outside of the spout into the tanks, while the majority puddled on the boat deck or ground.
The first issue observed was that the pressure required to activate (hold open) the self closing green swivel located at the lower portion of the spout combined with the location of the two tabs used to apply the pressure to the spout caused the spout to flex at the joint between the gas can and the spout.  This flexing resulted in the o-ring/gasket attached to the spout assemble to become dislodged.  Once dislodged, the fuel leaked from between the gas can and spout.  On several occasions, the spout assembly was removed the from the gas can and the o-ring/gasket re-positioned to its proper location. After additional uses, three of the four o-rings/gaskets developed a tear.  This further increased the amount of fuel leaking from between the gas can and spout assembly.

The second issue is related to the green self closing swivel.  The issue seems to be caused when partial pressure is removed.  This allow the swivel to move to a position between open and locked closed. Once pressure is reapplied to activate (hold open) the spout, the green swivel dislodges and becomes stuck in the full open or locked position.  Of the four spout assemblies, two are locked in the open position making transportation in a vehicle hazardous.
 
As noted the gas cans were used approximately six times.   Of the four spout assemblies, there remains only one semi-functioning unit.  This spout assembly  has the one remaining o-ring/gasket that has not developed a tear.  Unfortunately, the green self closing swivel is stuck in the open position.
justification: Potential fuel spills and stuck open spouts pose a significant risk of fire or explosion, but no injuries have been reported.

incident_description:
At about 2000 on 21 Jan '13 I lit a fire in my wood stove.  The lighter was placed about 8' from the stove to be used to ignite the next fire.  This lighter had been in use since about 1 Dec 2012 and was approximately 1/2 empty.  It had been purchased at Dollar General.  I have been storing lighters there since purchasing this home in Jan 2006 without incident.  At about 2130 we heard an explosion in the living room.  It sounded like a small caliber gun being discharged in our  concrete and steel dome home! 

We had previously noticed that some of our firewood had to be discarded due to someone having shot into the wood.  Shells were clearly visible in the bark a few pieces of firewood.  I assumed we had grabbed a piece of firewood with a shell in it and the shell had exploded in the wood stove.  

After removing family and pets to a safe place, I checked adjacent rooms to see if there was any sign of a shot.  Not finding anything, I cut the air to the stove to smother the fire and waited.  I examined the stove from a distance to see if any smoke was escaping from a new hole.  When none was found, I got closer and reexamined it.  The stove was intact.  I searched the room for the source of the explosion and found what was left of the A-Liter about 6' from it's point of origin!  It might have traveled further but it hit a stone wall in a corner, fell to the stone floor, and was stopped.  

I did NOT feel safe having these in my home any longer.  As I had bought a two pack, the unused one was removed to a rocky area outdoors with no vegetation or other combustibles, away from the goat, and left them outside overnight.  

On 01/22/2013 at approximately 1700, I called the Bloomfield Fire Department dispatch and explained what happened and asked if they would take both lighters and safely destroy or safely dispose of the unused one and examine the one that exploded.  They had a Fire Fighter meet me at the FD.  I turned in the exploded lighter parts and the unused lighter.  

The A-Liter that exploded was separated into an "V" shape and a separate part that had been the tank.  Both sections had wires.  The "V" was missing the metal sheath from the end that lights.  The screws that hold the two halves together were blown out and have not yet been located.  It was still joined at the tip by the interior molded plastic.  There were no identifying logo's or manufacturers stamps on the pieces we recovered.  If I hadn't purchased a two pack, I would have been unable to contact anyone.

I can only imagine what would have happened if the tank had been full or if it had landed on burnables such as carpet, furniture, or paper or if it had exploded when we were asleep or outdoors.

This is unacceptable and unsafe!  Beacon Power's website indicates this product is Made in China.
justification: Although no injuries occurred, the explosion could have caused significant property damage or harm if it had happened when the homeowners were asleep or if the lighter had landed on combustible materials.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that she has been purchasing these lighter for a few months and they all display the same failure.  The top part fell apart while she was attempting to use it, she did not receive any injury, however, it is very dangerous and should be investigated.

The manufacturer was not contacted as yet.

The consumer feels that this lighter should be recalled.

incident_description: On November 11, 2012, a bottle of Marshall [Gardens] PatioGlo Bio-Fuel Gel exploded while being poured into an un lit pot of a ceramic container on [REDACTED] back porch.  The ceramic container contained two separate pots and It was made specifically for fuel-gel.  The other pot in the container was lit while the fuel gel was being poured into the empty pot.  While the fuel-gel was being poured into the empty pot, the vapors of the gel ignited and flashed back into the bottle causing the bottle of gel-fuel to explode -- spewing the napalm-like gel all over [REDACTED] body, clothes and the porch furniture.  The gel stuck to and incinerated [REDACTED] clothes, skin, and the porch furniture.  [REDACTED] has 3rd and 2nd degree burns over 40% of her body, and she remains in ICU in the burn unit.  [REDACTED] is still on a ventilator and has had six surgeries to date.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injuries (3rd and 2nd degree burns over 40% of the body) and is likely to occur again due to the highly flammable nature of the fuel gel and the presence of an open flame.

incident_description:
bernzomatic premium flexible lighter bzltr300r. when refilling with supplied butane refill cartridge, the lighter refill valve stuck open, spraying out all of the butane until it was empty. if there had been an open flame or a cigarette lit anywhere in the room it would have caused a fire in my house.

justification: The stuck refill valve could have caused a fire, posing a significant risk to life and property.

incident_description:
On the morning of July 16, 2012, the female consumer was burning trash in a fifty-gallon drum her family uses to burn trash items.  It was early in the morning and the dew was still on the ground.  The consumer started the fire without using any accelerant, but a bottle of Diamond Brand Natural Fire Starter Gel was sitting in a plastic bucket on the ground roughly four to five feet away from the fifty-gallon drum.  Diamond Brand Natural Fire Starter Gel is an ethanol based fire starter with a gelling agent added to make it a thicker and more viscous gel.  This fuel gel product is similar, if not identical, to the fuel gel used with the fire pot products which have been recalled by the CPSC.
  After the fire had started, something in the burn barrel ÃÂpoppedÃÂ causing debris and hot coals to scatter into the air.  It is believed that a hot coal or other fire remnant landed on or near the bottle of Diamond Brand Natural Fire Stater Gel, causing the bottle to explode upon the consumersÃÂ body.  The flaming, napalm-like gel adhered to the consumersÃÂ body; melting her skin and causing severe burns over the majority of her body, limbs, and face.  Because the product was a gel, the flames were not easily extinguished.  The consumer was flown via [REDACTED] to the nearest burn unit for treatment.  She spent several months in the burn unit and barely survived the ordeal.  She is still receiving treatment and remains severely scarred from her burns.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns over the majority of the consumer's body, limbs, and face, with the gel product's napalm-like nature making it difficult to extinguish.

incident_description: cig. ligher self ignited after using it to light candles.  I went to put out the flame; ( 1 foot in height) and the lighter exploded extinguishing the fire.

incident_description:

incident_description:
Caller is reporting a transfer pump that is labeled multi use that transfers liquid from one source to another such as gasoline or oil.

When pump was manufactured, it was made without any way to screw together or clamp, it's just a plastic head that pushes into rubber head.
Container is plastic and has the raised area where the two halves are fused together & this is where the problem lies because it is not beaded correctly allowing leakage.
It is made to disasemble easily but the marks on it are a little bit raised and because gasoline is thin it leaks out of the bottom of the pump and leaks around feet of person using it.

He states that through the day the person using it can see the leaking but if it were to be used at night with vision impaired then it could be an extreme safety hazard.

Caller states that the verbiage states, that it is used to transport gasoline. 

When using this pump with gasoline
justification: Leakage of gasoline poses a fire hazard, especially in vision-impaired conditions.

incident_description:
I bought 2.5 gallon plastic gasoline cans for the first time in years due to the storm Sandy.  These cans come with a safety spout that I found nearly impossible to use.  To open the spout, you are supposed to push in and turn.  I couldn't get the spout positioned correctly so the gasoline would flow.  In fact, in all the cans I used, approximately 6, only one worked properly.
The result was that I found myself and the others using the cans removing the spout and trying to pour directly into the generators.  In some cases we did have a funnel, in others the gasoline spilled.
Mentioning this to my 90 year old mother, who still mows her grass on a riding mower, she told me she can't use the spout, so she takes it off and pours the gasoline in a glass jar and puts it in the mower with a funnel.
This spout is less safe than the older, open spout version.  It is less safe because it is complex and to hard to operate.  People are quickly frustrated and remove it, increasing the chances of spillage and fire.  I plan to remove them and replace them with an open spout.

[REDACTED] Professional Engineer
justification: The complex and difficult-to-use spout increases the likelihood of gasoline spills and potential fire incidents.

incident_description: use of Blitz 1 gallon gas can model 1+hand E flo Item # 85005. I was using the gan to refill a chain saw when I had to release the fluid lock with both hands.  Once I released the lock and slid the bar down a rush of gasoline squirted out of the can into my face.  I was extremely fortunate that I was wearing goggles at the time and prevented any direct contact with my eyes.  I still needed to go to the emergency room to have my eyes flushed for some contact but it was no where as severe as it could have been if not for the safety goggles.  To be very honest if I was not using a chain saw there is a good chance that I may not have been using safety googles.  I could have been wearing safety glasses or even very possible nothing to protect my face from a splash or eye impact.  I have never heard of or even seen this happen with a gas can before.  I personally believe that that the vapors built up rushed out causing a suction action pulling the gas out much like a whales spout.  Please note that I was not wearing the goggles correctly at the time and that is a minor point in this compliant considering the unusual event of using a simple gas can.
justification: Injury occurred due to unexpected gas squirt, but safety goggles mitigated severity.

incident_description:
Three year old  Blitz 5 gallon Red Plastic gasoline container split open and dumped 4 of 5 gallons of gasoline on the ground.  No injuries, and no fire.  The container was just setting there sealed storing gasoline. It was Not filled past the FILL line.   My opinion is the warn weather causes gasoline vapors to expand  resulting in excess pressures on the aging plastic containers.   4 to 5 gallons of gasoline dumping out unexpected from a container bursting is very dangerous.   

Blitz, Miami, Oklahoma, is aware of this defect as they replaced a container for me about a year ago.  They are all about the same age and either the plastic deteriorated from the fuel or the plastic is of inadequate strength for the additional pressures of warm day expansion.  

I did a search on the web for Blitz to contact them again about another container bursting apart, but I find the company is out of business from product liability law suits.
justification: Although no injuries occurred this time, the likelihood of future incidents is high due to the company's history of similar container failures.

incident_description: We recently purchased a "safety fuel can" for unleaded regular gasoline.  We were told the normal, regular gas cans were no longer available.  We took the can home, put gasoline in it, put gas in my mower, and placed the gas can in the shade until we needed it again.  The temperature was about 75 degrees.  The gas can swelled up and when we let off the pressure, fuel and vapors burst from the can.  If this had been my son, it could have been in his face.  This so called "safety can" has no vent to let off pressure.  This is more dangerous than pouring gas out on the ground.  We have thrown out this can and returned to using our old can as this one is more dangerous than any other can on the market.  At least our traditional fuel can won't explode in the back of the truck on the way home from the gas station.
justification: The gas can swelled up and burst, posing a high likelihood of injury if it had happened while in use.

On September 10, 2012, my gas water heater caught on fire on the gas pipe that leads  to the water heater.  Only during the fire did any smell occur.  For the last week, I have been experiencing headaches, stomach aches and tiredness as well as my 2 grandchildren who live we us.  My husband checked out gage on the propane tank and we had approximate 20% gas lost from the leak.  AmeriGas is taking the position that their gas has an odor to it, however the remaining gas is in the tank and it does not have an odor.  If an odor was present, we would not have been sicken nor would my home also had burn down, luckily I was home and was able to shut the gas off and put the fire out.

The pot exploded into a fireball and shot burning gel onto me and the love seat I was sitting on. The gel stuck to my arms and clothing, continuing to burn and ignite my clothing. I moved to the grass and my husband pushed me down and laid on top of me to extinguish the flames. My husband and neighbor continued to pat the flames until the fire was fully extinguished. The love seat was also completely burned. My husband had a minor burn on his chest from helping me. The fire and EMT personal were called, and I was flown by helicopter to Columbia (Missouri) Hospital Burn Center, were I was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns requiring ICU admission, making it a 'Injury' (3) and highly likely (4) to occur given the volatile nature of Napa fire gel.

incident_description:
Blitz Enviro-Flo Plus Plastic Gas Container is so well sealed (in a poor attempt to comply with 2009 enviromental laws) that the 5 gallon container swells up tremendously and rolls onto its side when exposed to summer heat in my garage.  These containers will do this regardless of whether they are full or empty. Obviously, having a full conatiner of gas laying on its side would be a significant fire/explosion risk if it began leaking.  

I understand the need to better seal the containers to safeguard the environment, however, the container must be redesigned to absolutely prevent it from swelling into a ball shape and rolling over.  A wider base; more substantial base molding; self-venting at some dangerous pressure.

The container should also be designed to relieve pressure automatically before the valve is opened - perhaps it could vent as a result of lifting the carry handle.
justification: The container's design flaw could lead to a significant fire/explosion risk if it leaks while on its side.

incident_description: The lighter was in the cigarette pack laying on a table. The lighter exploded while in the pack. Blew the lighter apart.

incident_description: Upon using American Match Strike 'N Lite cigarette lighter, the lighter exploded in my hand. Plastic shards from the ligher pierced my skin and scratched the paint on my car.

incident_description:
Purchased a  pack of (2) MK lighter brand lighters at a local convenience store. Put one in 
glove box in car for spare One morning, I got up, left my hotel room on the way to work and
could not find my lighter to light a cig. I suddenly remembered my spare in the glove box.

 What if I would have came out to my car and it was burnt to the ground? or What if the lighter
blew-up while I was driving down the road causing a fatal accident to me or other vehicles

incident_description:
The consumer wanted to illustrate some of her concerns about a disposable lighter ruptured while it sat in the consumerÃÂs car, over a span of 2 hours. incident_description:
The consumer stated that the gasoline container design is faulty.  The spout on the container is not long enough which causes the gasoline to spill.  In doing so he had lost half of the contents on the ground.

The consumer stated that he had attempted to use several other gas containers, which prove to be the same results.   He feels that this design needs to be redesigned for the safety of consumers and to prevent spillage.

incident_description: Blitz USA 5-Gallon Enviro-Flo Plus Gas Can is the worst gas can I have ever used. I have three. Two five gallon and one 2.5 gallon. All have the same faulty spout. All leak all the time. The five gallon containers are cumbersome to use. The spouts are just the right size to get stuck in the gas tank of a car. These cans are absolutely horrible. It is NOT possible to use won without spilling. The gas leaks through the mechanism, not at the can seal ot the flimsy spout. incident_description:
Purchased package of eleven cigarette lighters.

incident_description:
I live in an off-grid location and depend on gasoline generators for electric power.  This requires me to buy gasoline in 5 gallon cans on a regular basis.  Until several years ago, it was possible to buy different models at different stores.  However, 3 or 4 years ago, all the stores in Hawaii phased out all but one model.  The brand name is Blitz.  This manufacturer now has almost a total monopoly on the sale of gas cans--at least in the Sate of Hawaii.

These red, plastic cans cost anywhere from about $15 to $25, and it has annoyed me that they last only about 6 months before they develop pin-hole leaks.  In fact, it is more than annoying, it is dangerous.  I have often come home to find that a recently purchased can has leaked gasoline all over the bed of my pick-up truck because the leak was too small to notice at the gas station.  I have also gone into my storage shed on numerous occasions to find that relatively new cans have slowly leaked onto the floor of my shed.  This has degraded the bed of my truck and the floor of my shed, but the larger issue is that of the fire hazard.

I generally save the old cans with leaks until I have 5 or 6 of them that have all of the fuel gone from them and then take them to the local dump.  But today, I came home to find that a can I had just filled, and had only been used several times previously, was spurting gasoline all over my pick-up bed again on the 10 mile trip home.  The last time I filled up the cans, I was eating in a restaurant before going home when the waitress pointed out the window at liquid dripping out of the back of my truck.  Gasoline!

I have learned to check the cans regularly--especially when I fill them and before putting them in my shed--but these pin hole leaks can develop at any time.  I thought that it must be small stones or cinders that were causing the problem when the cans were weighted down with gasoline, so I put a plywood sheet in the bed of my truck and took care to sweep it clean of all debrise before loading the cans.

Today, after discovering a virtually new can had sprung a leak in my truck, I emptied it into another can and then pulled all the discarded cans I still had out to inspect them.  In every case the small pin holes were easy to identify by looking at the bottom of the cans or holding them up to the daylight and looking through the fill hole to see the bottom of the can from the inside.  And in every case, the holes were exactly the same.  They were not jagged or ragged like a stone would produce.  They were all about the size of a pin head or smaller and they were all perfectly round almost like they had been stamped out.  And they were not all on the very bottom of the can where a stone or bit of metal might puncture a hole.  Some of them were several centimeters above the bottom of the can.

It seems obvious that these cans are either purposely designed to spring leaks in order to shorten their useful life and sell more cans--which would be dangerous and unethical, given that they are designed solely for storing and transporting highly flamable gasoline. Or they are poorly manufactured with plastic walls that are too thin to be safe and perhaps have small air bubbles in them--which could maybe somehow explain the consistently and perfectly round holes that develop after a short time--which is, none-the-less, dangerous.

I believe that some testing of these cans should be done to confirm my conclusions and suspicions.  There must be many other people out there with similar experiences.  I myself have gone through about twenty cans in just a few years time.  I can't say what's available in other states but I would guess that since all the big box stores sell exactly the same model that the monopoly probably exists in the whole country. I believe the manufacturer must be aware of this flaw (if not outright causing it) and should be held accountable to correct it. This is not only a consumer rip-off but a dangerous problem.
justification: Regular incidents of gasoline leaks pose a significant fire hazard and risk of injury.
